Hi [~accountid:61b9ad7c2900b00071da0b68] ,

Feedback from Mazars TR:

_Actions that need be completed to be compliant by 15.01.2026 are_

_I.                    A new tax filling needs to be activated by an appointment from the tax office and official petition._

_II.                  After the filling platform is activated, the relevant information would need to be calculated and filled accordingly.,_

_III.                Assuming that Bolt TR is the only entity your group has shares in Turkey(Please confirm), we are currently in the conclusion that one of the safe harbour methodologies will need to be chosen and correctly declared on the filling._

_The service fee for current clients that are already working with Forvis Mazars in Turkey is_ *_750 Euros + VAT._*
_If the client is not within the limits of assumptions above, then a separate more detailed proposal is required._

Let me know I can confirm and kick off the process.

We had negotiated for some amendments to the CGV, which are visible in the “Informations Complémentaires”.

Please could we request the same amendments to these two new Terms of Sale?

These are: 

”Si ajustement de patrimoine à la baisse en cours de campagne, une solution devra être trouvée entre les deux parties afin de compenser la perte. 

Une permission écrite sera nécessaire avant utilisation des contenus dans un but documentaire et/ou marketing. 

L'article 9 des CDG "Droit d'exploitation du contenu numérique" ne s'appliquera pas sur ce contrat.”

For additional protection, I would ask for the following to be added as well: 

_“Les logos utilisés dans la campagne demeurent la propriété exclusive de Bolt et ne pourront être exploités en dehors du contrat sans autorisation écrite.”_

Given the amounts, please could you confirm that you have sought the approval of Julien Mouyeket to launch these campaigns? 

Thank you !

[~accountid:712020:548c71a6-d1f4-404d-9c5e-482bc0de371a], I reviewed the DPA and flagged the following privacy concerns:

* *Indemnity & Liability* 

Liability is fully subject to the Terms’ caps; no carve‑outs for data protection breaches. 6 months fees does not provide reasonable cover for breach of confidentiality, data protection obligations, and security incidents/regulatory fines.

* *Training models*

DPA does not contain *explicit prohibition* on training models on Client Data. Annex 2 mentions “Controls for Implementing AI/ML,” but this is programmatic, not a contractual use restriction. Absent a ban, “provide and maintain the Services” could be interpreted to include product improvement/feature development. We need to ask for a contractual prohibition on using Client Data for model training or third‑party AI unless explicitly opted‑in.

* *Unilateral Changes to the DPA*

Pipedrive may *unilaterally modify* the DPA “_to comply_” or to “_reflect changes in its data processing practices_,” effective upon *posting*; continued use = acceptance. We should sign a separate DPA and do not rely on online terms.

* *Personal Data Breach* 

Notice timeline: “Without undue delay (*targeted* notification time of no greater than 72 business hours)”. Risk: “_Targeted_” is non‑binding and “Business hours” can stretch beyond GDPR expectations (72 hours). Hard cap of 48 hours (not business hours) is preferred.

* *Data Storage*

We need to confirm if data is stored at rest for EEA clients. Is EU data residency available and default?

We would like to request your review of the attached approval form for the Priority Support Fee (“PSF”) in Cyprus and your confirmation on whether the fee is feasible from a FinReg perspective. Below is a summary of the fee, the purpose behind it, and the legal assessment received so far.

The PSF is intended for Bolt Business riders in Cyprus and would be charged by Bolt Operations OÜ. It applies only to Bolt Business rides and is meant to recover costs associated with providing enhanced business support services to corporate users. The fee is ultimately borne by the corporate client, although the invoice is addressed to the passenger. The business goal is to improve service quality by supporting access to higher-quality car categories and drivers with better performance metrics.

External counsel has confirmed that there is no explicit legal restriction under Cypriot law preventing implementation of the PSF. However, they highlighted a possible regulatory risk: even though the fee would be charged by Bolt and not by the taxi driver, the Road Transport Authority could take the view that it amounts to a supplement to the regulated taxi fare. This is relevant because taxi drivers may only charge fares approved by the Minister of Transport.

To mitigate this risk, external counsel recommends ensuring that the fee is clearly presented as a separate, platform-level charge, itemised in the app interface, retained entirely by Bolt, and not affecting driver pay or the regulated fare. It should also be framed as relating to non-transport support services and provided with full price transparency before booking. The fee definition and proposed T&Cs wording have been reviewed and endorsed by external counsel.

In summary, the legal risk is not zero but can be managed with the proposed safeguards. From a legal standpoint, we are comfortable proceeding if the business team is aligned. As a next step, we would appreciate FinReg’s review of the approval form and confirmation on whether you can give your greenlight to the fee setup or if further adjustments are required.

Please let us know if you need any additional information.

Many thanks!

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is currently partnered with Circle K, as part of Bolt Rewards.
** Previous ticket on this is [+LSS-34446+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-34446] (Estonia), which Gab advised on.
*** As part of discussions, Ops flagged that “_we used to have a pan-Baltic agreement with Circle K covering EE, LV, and LT_”. This contained a DSA which classified the parties as ICs. *This is the main agreement for current purposes*, and indicates a IC relationship (even though joint controllership was separately agreed for EE).
** Bolt promotes Circle K’s services to Bolt drivers, and Circle K provides the drivers with discounts on fuel / related services.
*** To benefit from Circle K’s discounts, drivers would use a link (provided by Circle K, but available on the Bolt Offers page) to create an account. This link would result in the discount being automatically applied, since it was API integrated.
* Recently, Bolt drivers have started to contact us flagging that they are unable to register with Circle K via the link. This is because the API integration no longer works, and Circle K will not be able to fix it until early spring next year.
** Circle K’s proposed interim solution is for Bolt to provide a weekly sheet of newly registered Bolt drivers with their phone numbers, so that Circle K can manually apply the discounts on the drivers' accounts.
*** Ops does not appear to be a fan of this idea, given that: (a) it is operational effort to provide a weekly list of new drivers; and (b) there will be existing drivers that want to create accounts with Circle K. As such, this seems like a non-starter.
** Instead, Ops are proposing adding a Google Form in the offers section, to collect data on drivers trying to register, and provide Circle K with the phone numbers of those drivers.
* *Request*: Can we proceed with the temporary Google Form setup?

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Google Form:
** This certainly seems more proportionate from a data minimisation perspective - Sharing the details of all new drivers is too much / does not make sense. Otherwise, the data sharing here seems low risk, particularly where the drivers have actively expressed an interest in getting involved with the discounts ✅ 
** Purpose of processing is to facilitate Bolt Rewards, legal basis likely to be LI. This is covered in the driver privacy notice ✅ 
** The only small gap is transparency regarding the recipient - this can easily be addressed in the Google Form (including a link to the PN) ⚠️ 
*** “_By providing your contact information via this form, Bolt will share it with Circle K Lietuva, UAB (and its affiliated companies) based on Bolt’s legitimate interest in facilitating your participation in the Bolt Rewards Programme. For more information on how your personal data is processed, please see our privacy notice available at_ [_https://bolt.eu/lt-lt/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides_|https://bolt.eu/lt-lt/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides]”
* Data Sharing Agreement: This covers the proposed data sharing ✅ 
** Between Lithuanian entities. Contains our standard IC DSA, with a mutual indemnity.
** Annex 1 lists Bolt as the data exporter, and includes driver name/phone number among categories of data being exchanged. 
* For completeness, worth also including the usual flags re direct marketing, as these were not flagged on the previous ticket 💡 

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Does this apply specifically to Lithuania, or other countries as well?
* Advice:
** DSA covers the proposed data sharing, which sounds fine to me.
** Google Form should include the above disclaimer language - I should review the form before it goes live.
** The usual marketing advice applies.

** No need for consent to send these comms, as unlikely to trigger direct marketing rules.
* Recording: ⚠️ 
** (1) Bolt employees (presenters): Name and video.
*** I highly doubt this will be an issue, but worth double-checking that these employees are ok with the recording being shared (as a *courtesy*). Ultimately, the data sharing is very low risk, particularly as the drivers have seen this information already, so should be fine.
** (2) Participants (via Slido): Name (usually just first name (x2), but on one occasion full name).
*** IMO, it would be disproportionate effort to take any steps relating to the first names. There are only two, and it is nearly impossible for the other drivers to identify who the first names apply to, so we can leave this as is.
*** The only possible concern is the one full name. This is not covered in our driver privacy notice (the closest we come is survey/interview data, which is not a good fit) and I highly doubt the driver was informed in advance (there is not even a mention of the session being recorded) - As such, the risk here is that sharing the name would exceed the driver’s expectations (although the overall risk profile is low here, particularly as the drivers have already seen it).
**** In an ideal world, we would *redact* this from the video if at all possible - this would allow us to sidestep most of the privacy risks.
**** If we cannot redact this, then we should not rely on consent - it would be disproportionate to tank the whole recording if the driver objected. Instead, we can take the following approach:
***** INTERNAL:
****** (i) Argue the processing is compatible with the original purpose (i.e., giving the drivers access to the content they already saw),
****** (ii) Rely on legitimate interest (i.e., providing drivers with continued access to training information). Sharing is necessary as re-recording would be disproportionate, and the balancing test is met here.
****** (iii) Argue that sharing the recording is within the driver’s reasonable expectations. This is the main risk, but we can probably find something to rely on here.
***** EXTERNAL:
****** (iv) Consider sharing a *courtesy comm* saying that the recording is only shared with those who attended (and should not be reshared), and is based on Bolt’s legitimate interest in providing follow-up access to the training (this should address the transparency gap).
****** (v) Ensure that the link *cannot be shared publicly*.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** How many drivers attended the webinar?
* Advice:
** Option A: Redact the full name from the video, if possible.
** Option B: Send the recording and replace the Slido section with written Q&A / audio only.
** Option C: Send the recording as-is, but with some disclaimer language, and accept the (admittedly limited) risk.

Under Danish road traffic and taxi regulation, primary liability for this type of bodily injury rests with the _vognmand_ / fleet operator (FO) as the user of the vehicle, and with their motor / third-party liability insurer. Any fault attributable to the driver is legally imputed to the FO and is covered by the FO’s insurance. Bolt, as a dispatching platform and contractual reseller of the service, is generally not a direct addressee for compensation claims unless independent fault by Bolt can be demonstrated (e.g., Bolt knew about a specific defect in this vehicle and failed to act).

Accordingly, the passenger should be directed straight to the FO’s liability insurer. It is both legally and practically appropriate to provide the passenger with the name of the vognmand’s insurer, the policy/customer number, and the claims contact details—while ensuring no excessive personal data is shared (e.g., no CPR number).

Hi [~accountid:712020:5960c3dd-0f70-4ba3-bd49-119c42bd10e5] - thanks for looping me in. {color:#4c9aff}*Do we know roughly how many drivers attended the webinar*{color} (and therefore how many would receive the comms/recording? (?) This will give me a better understanding of the overall risk profile.

Ultimately, it looks like +three+ driver names appear in the recording (two first names, and one full name). In light of this, as well as the fact that the attendees have already seen these names when they attended the webinar, {color:#36b37e}*the overall privacy risk is low*{color} here 🙌  Nevertheless, you are right to flag this as a risk - since it appears that the webinar does not mention how the session is being recorded and may later be shared, the risk is that the relevant drivers could complain that sharing their names in this way is beyond what they would reasonably expect ⚠️ As such, we should try and take some steps to address this.

----

:ladder: In terms of how to address the risk, we largely have two options:

* 💡 *Option A* (lowest risk, but most effort): *Remove the driver names from the recordings*.
** This could be done by either: (a) redacting the names from the recording; or (b) cutting out the Slido section of the recording and replacing it with audio only (or a written Q&A).
** I confess I am not familiar with what is possible here from a technical POV, and so it is worth asking the stakeholders. If it is possible to achieve without too much operational strain, then this would be the best option as it eliminates the core privacy risk.
* 💡 *Option B* (slightly more risky, but pragmatic): *Provide the recording as-is, but include some disclaimer language in the comms and deploy some safeguards to prevent re-use.*
** If there is no way to remove the names from the recording (or if it is too much effort), IMO it would be disproportionate to use this as grounds to not share the recording at all. As I have said above, the processing here is ultimately low risk, and we have good reasons for wanting to share the recording. As such, we could instead take a risk-based approach and take some steps to try and _mitigate_ (not eliminate) the risk of complaints (provided that the business is willing to accept this risk).
** The main step we could take here would be to *include some language in the comms* to: (a) provide drivers with transparency information about what and how we are sharing their personal data in this context; and (b) provide them with reassurances that their data is secure. Such language could look something like the following:
*** “_This recording is only being shared with the webinar participants, and should not be forwarded or re-shared. To the extent that the recording contains any limited participant personal data, Bolt processes such data based on its legitimate interest in providing drivers with ongoing access to relevant training sessions. Further information on how Bolt processes personal data can be found in our privacy notice available on the website_.”
** For good order, we should also take steps to ensure that: (1) the recording cannot be shared publicly (i.e., it can *only be shared with the participants*); and (2) the recording is *not published by us in any marketing / promotional materials*. This would limit the risk profile significantly.

----

Hi Ivan 

I’ve now reviewed the Flex communications and webinar from a legal perspective and, overall, they look fine to use, subject to making some small adjustments. I’ve summarised the key points below.

Although Flex operates under an agency model — which supports driver independence — some of the current wording in the comms (e.g., “master bidding strategies”, “maximise your earnings”) sounds prescriptive and could create a legal reclassification risk, as it may suggest that Bolt is directing how drivers should operate. This risk is low in practice and can be easily addressed with a few small wording changes:

* Use more *informational* rather than instructional language (e.g., “overview of how Bolt Flex works”).
* Highlight that *drivers are fully free* to choose how they set prices and use Flex.
* Avoid strong earnings claims.

I’ve suggested alternative phrasing directly in the comms document.

On the webinar recording, the reclassification risk is *low*, provided the recording is clearly framed as *informational only* when shared. To reinforce the informational nature of the recording, it would be helpful to include a short autonomy disclaimer when circulating it, for example: _“This material is provided for information only. Drivers remain fully free to choose how they set prices and use Bolt Flex.”_

Separately, there are some *privacy considerations*, as driver names appear in the Q&A segment. I’ve already looped in [~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] to look into this and asked him to come back to you directly.

Let me know if you have any questions or you'd like me to review updated drafts once the changes are made.

Point 5.4: “Alternative solutions are not permitted” — Is it unfair and potentially biased? Do you have the right to make that argument?

Yes — you *do* have the right to argue that this clause is unfair, discriminatory, and potentially tailored for a specific vendor. Below is a clear legal reasoning you can rely on.

----

h1. 1. *Do you have the right to claim that the ban on alternative solutions is biased / disproportionate?*

*Yes.*

Under the Public Procurement Act (RHS) and relevant EU case law:

* technical specifications must be *non-discriminatory*,
* the contracting authority *must not artificially restrict competition*,
* requirements must be *proportionate* to the legitimate objective.

If the procurement requires a very specific service model (traditional taxi service with taximeter, printed receipts, taxi permits, etc.) _and explicitly forbids_ all alternative but equivalent technological solutions (like platform-based services), then:

h3. ✔ *It unjustifiably restricts competition*

Modern service providers like Bolt Business are excluded.

h3. ✔ *It may indicate that the tender is tailored to a specific vendor*

Especially in a market with only a few operators that match such old-style requirements.

h3. ✔ *It violates RHS § 89(1)* — technical specifications must allow equivalent solutions if they achieve the same outcome.

h3. ✔ *An absolute prohibition of alternatives is not lawful unless strictly justified*

The contracting authority must prove that only the traditional taxi model can meet its needs — which is practically impossible, since digital logs provide *greater traceability* than a taximeter.

Thus — *yes, your argument is legally sound and strong*.

----

h1. 2. *Legal arguments supporting the claim that point 5.4 is disproportionate / biased*

h3. *2.1 RHS § 3(2) — Principle of promoting competition*

The authority must maximize competition.
A ban on alternatives *artificially narrows the market*.

h3. *2.2 RHS § 88 / § 89 — Technical specifications must not discriminate*

* The contracting authority must not describe the service in a way that fits only one type of supplier.
* Equivalent solutions *must* be permitted.

h3. *2.3 EU Court of Justice jurisprudence — the “equivalence principle”*

Authorities may not reject modern technological solutions if they provide the same functionality (e.g., digital trip logs vs printed taximeter receipts).

h3. *2.4 RHS § 4(1) — Proportionality principle*

Requirements must be:

* necessary,
* suitable,
* and not excessive.

The combination of strict traditional taxi requirements + a total ban on alternatives suggests *clear disproportionality*.

h3. *2.5 Prohibition of favouring a specific vendor*

If the requirements align closely with only one or a few traditional taxi companies, the suspicion of *biased tendering* is justified and challengeable.

----

h1. 3. *Recommended wording (for a formal complaint / challenge)*

{quote}*We challenge the legality of point 5.4 (“Alternative solutions are not permitted”).*

This clause excludes all equivalent digital or platform-based service models, even though they fully meet the contracting authority’s needs (trip registration, transparency, reporting) — and often provide these at a higher technological standard than traditional taximeter-based taxi services.

Such an absolute prohibition:

* *unlawfully restricts competition*, contrary to RHS § 3(2);
* *is disproportionate* under RHS § 4, since the objective could be achieved through less restrictive means;
* *violates RHS § 89*, because it does not allow equivalent solutions and unjustifiably favours a narrow group of providers;
* *creates an impression that the tender conditions are tailored for a specific market operator*, contrary to the principles of transparency and equal treatment.

We request that point 5.4 be revised to allow equivalent technical solutions, as the current absolute prohibition results in a procurement that is disproportionately aligned with a single service model and unjustifiably excludes major segments of potential suppliers, including innovative platform-based transport providers.{quote}

bicycle weight is 36Kg. pedal height from ground is 467mm. How big is the impact to the pedal in case the bike falls over and the pedal hits concrete surface

h6. ChatGPT said:

Thought for 16s

Short answer: *it’s huge* – on the order of *tens of kilonewtons*.

Let’s estimate it.

----

h3. 1. Energy of the falling bike

* Bike mass m=36 kgm = 36\ \text{kg}m=36 kg
* Pedal height above ground h=0.467 mh = 0.467\ \text{m}h=0.467 m
* Gravity g=9.81 m/s2g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2g=9.81 m/s2

If the bike simply tips over from rest and the pedal hits the ground, the potential energy that turns into impact energy is roughly

E≈mgh=36⋅9.81⋅0.467≈1.65×102 JE \approx mgh = 36 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.467 \approx 1.65\times10^2\ \text{J}E≈mgh=36⋅9.81⋅0.467≈1.65×102 J

So about *165 joules* of energy has to be dissipated at impact (mostly through deformation of the pedal, crank, frame, and a tiny bit of concrete).

----

h3. 2. Converting energy to impact force

Average impact force can be approximated from work–energy:

E≈Favg⋅s⇒Favg≈EsE \approx F_{\text{avg}} \cdot s \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{\text{avg}} \approx \frac{E}{s}E≈Favg​⋅s⇒Favg​≈sE​

where sss = stopping distance (how much the system deforms/compresses during impact).

We don’t know sss exactly, so let’s look at a reasonable range:

||Assumed stopping distance sss||Estimated average impact force FavgF_{\text{avg}}Favg​||Approx. “kg of load” ( F/gF/gF/g )||
|2 mm (0.002 m)|~82,000 N|~8,400 kgf|
|5 mm (0.005 m)|~33,000 N|~3,400 kgf|
|10 mm (0.01 m)|~16,500 N|~1,700 kgf|

So even with 1 cm of “give,” you’re still talking *~16 kN* average force, and peak force will be higher than the average.

----

h3. 3. What this means in practice

* The pedal/crank sees an *impact equivalent to several tons of static load*, but only for a very short time.
* That’s why a simple tip-over can bend a pedal, crank arm, or derailleur even though the bike “only” weighs 36 kg.
* Exact force will depend heavily on:
** Where the bike’s center of mass actually is,
** Whether a tire or bar end hits first (sharing energy),
** Material stiffness of pedal, crank, frame, and ground.

If you tell me what type of pedal/crank (material, design) and whether any other parts hit first (handlebar, wheel, etc.), I can refine the model a bit, but the key takeaway is: *order of magnitude ~10–50 kN* depending on how much it deforms on impact.

h5. You said:

crank arm material is aluminum and heat treated to T6

h6. ChatGPT said:

Got it – so we’ve got:

* *Bike mass* ≈ 36 kg
* *Pedal height* ≈ 0.467 m
* *Crank arm*: heat-treated *aluminium T6* (most likely something like 6061-T6 or 7075-T6)

From the previous step we estimated the energy at impact:

E≈mgh≈36⋅9.81⋅0.467≈165 JE \approx mgh \approx 36 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.467 \approx 165\text{ J}E≈mgh≈36⋅9.81⋅0.467≈165 J

Using a reasonable deformation range (2–10 mm of “give” at the pedal + crank):

* 2 mm stop → ~82 kN avg force
* 5 mm stop → ~33 kN avg force
* 10 mm stop → ~16.5 kN avg force

Real value will probably sit *somewhere in that band*, depending how stiff the system is and what else hits the ground.

----

h2. What T6 aluminium means for the crank

Typical T6 aluminium crank materials:

* *6061-T6*: yield strength ≈ 240–280 MPa
* *7075-T6*: yield strength ≈ 430–500 MPa

Crank designers know bikes fall over, so:

* The *cross-section* of the crank is sized so that *normal pedalling loads + occasional tip-over* don’t immediately snap it.
* However, those *lateral impact loads from a fall* are _not_ what the crank is most optimized for (it’s mainly designed for torque from pedalling).

With a lateral impact of *~20–30 kN* at the pedal and a crank length around *0.17 m*, the bending moment at the crank root is on the order of:

M∼F⋅L≈(20–30 kN)⋅0.17≈3.4–5.1 kN\cdotpmM \sim F \cdot L \approx (20\text{–}30\,\text{kN}) \cdot 0.17 \approx 3.4\text{–}5.1\ \text{kN·m}M∼F⋅L≈(20–30kN)⋅0.17≈3.4–5.1 kN\cdotpm

For a typical hollow forged crank, that kind of moment is *right around the range where you can get permanent bending or slight twisting*, especially at:

* The *pedal eye* (threads can ovalize or crack later),
* The *root near the spider/axle* where section transitions.

----

h2. So, “how big is the impact” in practical terms?

Putting it all together:

* *Order of magnitude*:
** *Average impact force at the pedal*: roughly *15–40 kN*
** Equivalent to *~1.5–4 tons* of static load.
* *T6 aluminium*:
** Strong enough that one fall usually doesn’t _snap_ the crank.
** But a hard fall can *bend the crank slightly*, *damage threads*, or create *micro-cracks* that may grow over time.

Hey [~accountid:5cca9996e494c810153b1b03] ! 
I would like to have your view on this topic, since it is a T&Cs related one.

Mine is that this is more a safety / expectation-management question than a legal one, and we should not write specifically in the T&Cs that couriers will or will not go inside buildings / hotels / hospital wards (it is better to keep the definition broad, as it is now. For example, if we clearly state in the T&Cs that couriers will go inside buildings, wards, rooms etc., we are creating obligations that may conflict with building rules, hospital policies, etc, and increase safety and liability risk for couriers (harassment claims, access to sensitive areas...).

I’d maybe add a clear *FAQ for eaters.* Something like:

*Where will my order be delivered?*
_By default, your courier will deliver your order to the main entrance, lobby, reception or another publicly accessible point at the Drop-Off Location you selected._

_Couriers are not required to enter private apartments, hotel rooms or hospital wards, especially where access is restricted or subject to security / health rules._

_If you need a specific handover point (for example “hotel reception”, “security gate”, “main entrance of hospital”), please write this in the delivery notes or agree it with the courier via chat or call, as long as it is safe, accessible and allowed by the building / hospital rules._

And at the same time an *internal guidance for couriers (via fleets or courier FAQS).* Something like:

* Always follow building and hospital rules, and respect security staff.
* You are not required to enter private apartments, hotel rooms or hospital wards.
* If you feel unsafe or access is restricted, ask the eater to meet you at the entrance, reception or other public access point.
* Use chat/call to agree a safe meeting point when the address is a large site (hospital, hotel, office complex, etc.).

But nothing more than this. WDYT?

Thank you!

Hey [~accountid:60bf49438f2cc1006972698a] ,

Thank you for the context provided.

From our view, this is mainly a safety and expectation-management issue rather than a legal issue.

From a legal perspective, we believe we should not amend the T&Cs to say explicitly whether couriers will or will not enter buildings, hotels or hospital wards. The current definition of Drop-off location is intentionally broad and works well as a contractual baseline.

If we started stating in the T&Cs that couriers will or will not go inside buildings/wards/rooms, we might be creating obligations that may conflict with building rules, hospital policies and security/health protocols, and increase safety and liability risk for couriers (e.g. access to sensitive areas, disputes in private spaces, harassment allegations, etc.).

T&Cs are also not the best place to regulate this type of very operational detail.

What we would recommend instead is that Courier Ops / CS Team to create a clear FAQ that sets expectations, and a correspondent internal / courier guidance. This should be enough to manage expectations and reduce complaints in similar situations, while avoiding additional obligations or risks for Bolt and the couriers.

The exact wording of the FAQ and courier guidance is very operational, so I’ll leave it to Courier Ops / CS Team, but I am happy to check it once you have a draft, if you want.

Thank you!

Thanks all - As Rachel mentioned, the only obvious privacy risk here is the *inclusion of driver names in the recording* (during the Slido section). Having watched the recording, at no point were the drivers told that the session was being recorded and could be later circulated (which ultimately should have happened) - When the recording is circulated to over 250 people, those drivers may argue that they were not aware that their names would be circulated in this manner ⚠️ Although the overall risk profile here is *low*, this could still result in driver complaints being sent to Bolt - we should therefore aim to take proportionate steps to mitigate this risk 💡 

In practical terms, this means that we have two options:

*Option* 🅰️ : Remove the driver names from the recording before circulating it.

* This would be the most compliant and lowest-risk approach.
* Although I confess I am unfamiliar how this would work from a technical POV, I would imagine it would involve either: (a) redacting the names from the recording; or (b) cutting out the Slido section of the recording and replacing it with audio only (or a written Q&A). If there is time, it would be worth exploring how easily we can achieve this - if it can be done easily, it is worth taking this option.
* Ultimately, it this would involve too much technical/operational strain (or cause disproportionate delays) then we can go with Option B.

*Option* 🅱️ : Provide the recording as-is, but include some language in the comms to reassure the drivers.

* This approach does not entirely eliminate the risk of complaints, but in the circumstances it could be a pragmatic middle ground. If the business is willing to accept that there is a risk that relevant drivers may complain to Bolt, then taking a risk-based approach, this is something we can do.
* If this option is chosen, then we should:

h2. *3.1 Contested point: the requirement to use a taximeter and a taximeter printer*

*Relevant sections of the procurement document:*

* The taxi driver must provide a receipt printed by a taximeter printer.
* Pricing must be based on a tariff structure (start fee + km tariff + time tariff).

*Problem for Bolt’s business model:*

* Bolt Business does not use a taximeter; instead, it relies on digital price calculation, a price known in advance, and an electronic trip report.
* No physical printed receipts are issued.

*Argument for the challenge:*
“ The procurement document requires the use of a physical taximeter and taximeter printer, as well as a pricing model consisting of a start fee, kilometre tariff and time tariff. Bolt Business relies on certified digital trip logs and electronic invoicing, which provide comparable or even greater transparency. Such a technical requirement may be unjustifiably restrictive within the meaning of RHS § 89(1), if the contracting authority’s objective — obtaining a transparent and verifiable trip record — can be achieved equally well with other technological solutions.”

----

h2. *3.2 Contested point: the requirement to have at least 50 vehicles with a taxi service permit (taksoveo sõidukikaart)*

*Problem for Bolt’s model:*

* Bolt does not own a taxi fleet – the platform intermediates rides.
* The platform does not own vehicles nor taxi permits.

*Argument for the challenge:*
“The requirement to have at least 50 vehicles registered for taxi service excludes providers that operate on the basis of licensed partners and a platform model (principle of promoting competition, RHS § 3(2)). The contracting authority’s aim is to ensure sufficient vehicle availability and service accessibility, which could also be achieved through alternative mechanisms (e.g., aggregate capacity of platform partners, response times, service availability SLAs). The requirement as currently formulated unjustifiably excludes a large proportion of market participants.”

----

h2. *3.3 Contested point: the requirement that the service must constitute taxi service in the legal sense*

*Problem for Bolt Business:*

* The procurement document requires a taxi service vehicle card, a driver service card, and a taximeter → this means a traditional taxi service rather than a platform-based pre-booked service.
* Bolt Business is an on-demand ride service platform, not a taxi service in the legal sense of taxi legislation.

*Argument for the challenge:*
“The contracting authority has chosen ‘taxi service’ as the service category, but the actual need may be for a pre-ordered ride service with invoicing. If the authority’s real need does not require compliance with the strict provisions of taxi legislation (taximeter, taxi permit, service card), the current choice of service type may conflict with the purposefulness principle under RHS § 4(1).”

----

h2. *3.4 Contested point: the requirement to issue a physical printed receipt*

*Problem:*

* Bolt issues digital receipts, not paper receipts printed using a physical printer.
* The digital log contains all required data (time, price, distance, route, etc.).

*Legal argument:*
“The obligation to issue a printed receipt disproportionately restricts technological solutions that provide the same information electronically. Under RHS § 89(1), technical specifications must be proportionate and must enable the use of different technologies when they achieve the same result.”

----

h2. *3.5 Contested point: rigidity of the pricing model*

The procurement allows only a taximeter-based tariff model, while Bolt uses:

* dynamic pricing,
* a fixed price known in advance.

*Argument for the challenge:*
“The procurement document requires a specific tariff-based pricing model (start fee + km + time), excluding models that could offer the contracting authority potentially more stable and predictable costs. Such a restriction may not be proportionate or aligned with the intended purpose.”

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Update 9 December 2025 - Quoting [~accountid:63b29b637cde7bff9d796748] ´s reply on refund deductions booking rationale within the ledger.


_As we previously discussed, the refunds to users can happen in two cases:_

* _when the courier is at fault -> cost is not deductible from courier balance. Booked straight to the PnL_
* _provider mistake -> cost might be deductible from the provider payouts. Even if landed to PnL, the net effect in the case of refund deductions is 0, which is why you've requested to have a pass-through balance to eliminate such cases when Bolt manages to deduct the refund from providers._  

_After evaluating the operational flow of restaurant refund recoveries, implementing a Balance Sheet pass-through account would not resolve the deductibility issue in practice and would materially increase manual workload._
*_Key points:_*

* _The timing of refund deduction to providers is not consistent, as it depends on Customer Support logic, manual adjustments by local operations, and potential provider disputes._
* _Refund deductions are not always triggered automatically, and in many cases they are delayed, disputed, or later reversed._
* _As a result, a pass-through account would require monthly detailed reconciliation, entirely manual, to track which refunds were:_
** _recovered from providers_
** _still pending_
** _reversed due to disputes_
** _unrecoverable_
* _Given this operational variability, there is a high likelihood that balances in the_ _BS pass-through account would accumulate and ultimately require manual write-offs._
* _Therefore, while a pass-through design is theoretically cleaner from a tax perspective, it does not work operationally in the current setup and would introduce:_
** _additional accounting complexity_
** _more manual interventions_
** _higher reconciliation risk_
** _without materially reducing non-deductible cost exposure_

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. Partner’s latest feedback regarding the open clauses:

There is no warranty provided regarding the API in clause 7.1. Please revise this clause and specify that a warranty is provided.

Regarding clause 8.2, I am providing the legal opinion below:

In the first sentence of clause 8.2, termination with 30 days’ prior written notice is envisaged. However, the following sentence states that, in the event of termination of this Agreement, other service agreements related to the use of the Bolt Food Platform may be terminated immediately with written notice. In such a case, the purpose of the 30-day notice period is lost. Since termination of the API Agreement grants the right to immediately terminate other agreements, the notice period is effectively not applied, resulting in an imbalanced termination procedure.

Additionally, we allocate resources for platform integration and operational readiness. Immediate termination of other agreements may cause significant difficulties in commercial operations. Therefore, termination of the API Agreement should not automatically result in the termination of other agreements.

Termination of the API Agreement should not lead to immediate termination of the other agreements; service agreements should be terminated only in accordance with their own terms, and the 30-day notice period should be effectively preserved.

There is a contradiction between the two agreements. Please ensure that the 30-day notice period is maintained in both agreements.

1)I added logic to the Google script to identify the structure of Notes. If the Notes contain two sections: *Summary* and *Transcription,* we send this data to the BR record, populating the fields *Gemini Notes* and *Transcription* (this field was newly added). If the Notes contain *multiple different sections*, all of this information will be stored in a single Salesforce field *Gemini Notes.* Example: [https://bolt-rides.lightning.force.com/lightning/r/BusinessReview__c/a03aA00000RxoCYQAZ/view|https://bolt-rides.lightning.force.com/lightning/r/BusinessReview__c/a03aA00000RxoCYQAZ/view]
2) Logging — It was very difficult to analyze why some notes weren’t being fetched, because this Google Script runs in the user’s environment and I can’t see their execution context. So I decided that it was time to implement a centralized logging system in our org.
I implemented the enterprise logger “Nebula” into Salesforce and updated the Google Script to send all logs, errors, and success messages to SF. So then I can collect a list of Gemini notes that have issues, and we can discuss the reasons with the AM.

** (ii) The link takes drivers to a Ignitis-run registration form. Drivers will need to fill in their name, contact details and ‘activity number’. Drivers will also check a box and confirm that Ignitis will provide them with personal offers and contact them if needed (they cannot proceed without it).
*** NB. Contact details are not strictly necessary - this is just in case the driver spells their name wrong.
*** NB. ‘Activity number’: Number needed by drivers in order to obtain a licence (it is available to riders in the app).
** (iii) Bolt will (on a monthly basis) share a list with Ignitis of active drivers using EVs. This list will include driver name, activity number, and email address  phone number.
** (iv) Ignitis then checks the list against drivers to match their registration form information. If it matches, Ignitis will create an account for the driver, where the driver can benefit from discounts. If it does not match, Ignitis will contact the driver directly to clarify.
* As part of this, we are relying on our usual partnership agreement, which contains a DSA ([LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wLfAN1Jr1bOLOnflD2zok47zoUja-Tiq/edit]).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Proportionality:
** We should only be sharing contact information if this is strictly needed ⚠️ Phone number is definitely not needed. Email address at a push, but only if actually needed.
** Equally, it is unclear why we are sharing lists of all EV drivers each month - this does not seem proportionate ⚠️ Surely there must be a way of limiting this to drivers that have expressed an interest in the offer.
** It sounds like Ignitis is forcibly demanding consent to marketing. Although not a direct issue for us, it could lead to complaints being (incorrectly) targeted at Bolt ⚠️  It would therefore be helpful to quickly check a copy of the form for anything obviously problematic.
* Data Sharing:
** DSA currently attached to the collaboration agreement is the Africa template. I have updated this ✅ 
*** Currently, it looks like the data sharing is one-way (Bolt is the sender). As such, full suite of protections should apply. If Ignitis pushes back, we can reconsider given that the data sharing is low risk.
* Marketing:
** Usual advice applies. Rely on opt-in consent for any targeted mediums ✅ 

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** What is the activity number called.
** Is the form managed and run by Ignitis?
** Why do we have to share a list of active drivers using EVs? Why does Ignitis not know the list of drivers from those who have used the form? Is there no way of limiting this to relevant drivers?
** Is Ignitis sharing any personal data with Bolt?
** Does this exclusively apply to Lithuania?
* Additional checks:
** Double-check we are ok to share individual activity number, but should be ok.
* Advice:
** Proportionality - Only share contact info if there is a compelling reason. Ideally do not share all drivers; only relevant ones. Can we check the form for anything obviously problematic?
** DSA - I have made some updates, given that it was the Africa template. Feel free to share with Ignitis.
** Marketing - If any targeted mediums used, we can only rely on opt-in consent.

I investigated the cases where the *Country of VAT origination (Supplier Country)* is empty. This field may be blank for any of the following reasons:

* The supplier does not have a primary tax ID in Workday.
* The supplier does not have any tax ID in Workday.
* The supplier does not have an address in Workday.
* The VAT originates not from a supplier invoice or supplier invoice adjustment, but from an expense report or account journal.

Hey [~accountid:618124ab3e3753006f742d1c] did a quick ChatGPT search:

Articles 12 and 13 indeed do not constitute a valid legal basis.



h3. *Article 12*

Article 12 regulates _powers of NACP_ for lifestyle monitoring of declarants.
However, it applies *only to declarants and public authorities*, not private businesses such as Bolt.
It does *not* contain a rule obliging companies to provide information.

h3. *Article 13*

This defines the role of agencies engaged in anti-corruption activities.
It does not impose obligations on private controllers to disclose data.



h3. *Article 51*

Article 51 regulates _monitoring of lifestyle_ of declarants.
Again, the duties fall on the _declarant_ and _public bodies_, not on private service providers.

Nothing in these articles states that:

* private companies must provide _any_ data;
* companies must verify existence of accounts;
* companies must disclose commercial service data.



In short, there are no disclosure duties on the companies about Declarants.

(?) Before providing my final advice, I would be grateful for answers to the following questions (?) 

# What is the specific name of the ‘activity number’ that you are referring to in LT? I just want to double-check whether there are any specific local law requirements regarding processing this datapoint.
# Presumably the registration form was created by, and is managed by, Ignitis? Is there any chance I could see a copy?
# Does this exclusively apply to Lithuanian drivers, and will the data only be exchanged between Bolt Ops OU and Ignitis' LT entity?
# I see that Bolt will be sharing personal data with Ignitis. Will Ignitis be sharing any personal data with Bolt (e.g., so that we can measure the effectiveness of this initiative)?
# Why do we need to share a monthly list of all EV drivers with Ignitis for Ignitis to be able to check driver registration details? Is there no way for us to share a list of just the drivers that have filled in the form, or alternatively can Ignitis not just record which people who have fulled in the form are Bolt drivers on their side? I just want to check that sharing lists of _all_ drivers is _strictly_ necessary here to achieve the intended purpose.

----

(i) Subject to the above (please confirm first), my advice will probably look like the following from a privacy POV (i) 

* *Data minimisation / proportionality*:
** I understand that it is not strictly necessary to share contact information with Ignitis. My preference would therefore be to not do so, as this is more compliant with the principle of data minimisation. If there is a compelling push to share contact information, we can consider sharing driver email addresses; however, it does not seem proportionate to share phone numbers.
** It is not clear to me why we need to share a monthly list of _all_ EV drivers with Ignitis. If there is an alternative option that would involve sharing less data while still achieving the same purpose, this would be preferable. However, ultimately, if this is the +_only_+ way of achieving the intended goal, then it is something we can do.
** We want to be careful in checking that Ignitis themselves are not doing anything obviously against data protection laws here. The reason for this is that since Bolt is the one introducing drivers to Ignitis, it is possible that disgruntled drivers will and their complaints to Bolt (as the most obviously user-facing party here), and so we want to do what we can to minimise the risk of complaints (this is why I would like to quickly check the registration form, if possible).
* *Data sharing agreement*: 
** I have edited to the DSA and related Appendices. I will finalise my edits once the above Qs are answered, and then the DSA will be ready to share with Ignitis.
* *Direct marketing*: 
** Since we will be promoting Ignitis' services to Bolt drivers, we need to be careful not to fall afoul of direct marketing requirements. ** If we are just promoting the offer via *_general / untargeted_* means (e.g., as a post on the Bolt offers page), we do not need to rely on consent.

* HTTP 503 code is returned

h2. *Audit Trail: Baker McKenzie Recommendations (TW MODA PDPA Compliance)*

*Source:* External Counsel Review - attached [^Bolt Taiwan MODA Guidelines Compliance Assessment — Summary & Assessment (for Baker McKenzie)_Confidentialprivileged_(BM 20251203).docx] 

----

*Summary of the Recommendations*

h3. *1. Self-Assessment Checklist (MODA Template 1) -* {color:#bf2600}*FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
 MODA expects a checklist directly aligned with the Regulations Governing Personal Data File Security Maintenance. None of Bolt’s existing documentation, including those such as the “Expansion Legal Memo”, do _not_ meet MODA’s required format or structure.
*Recommendations:*
* Adopt MODA’s official Self-Assessment Checklist template for Taiwan operations.
* Ensure each requirement is mapped and evidenced in checklist form (mandatory for MODA).
----
h3. *2. Personal Data File Security Maintenance Plan (Template 2)*
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt’s submission to MODA is acceptable; no follow-ups were received.
*Recommendations:*
* None at this stage.
----
h2. *3. Personal Data Inventory Form (Template 3)* {color:#bf2600}*- FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt’s RoPA is generally aligned with MODA expectations. The substance is sufficient, but the following enhancements are advisable.
*Recommendations:*
Add *new fields* into RoPA:
* Confirmation of *privacy notice provision* per processing activity.
* Description of *data deletion/destruction method*.
* Explicit field indicating *outsourcing to processors*.
* *Localized data subject rights* (exclude non-PDPA rights such as portability/ADM).
* Optional but recommended: include references to official PDPA *purpose codes* and *data category codes*.
* Apply *consistent fields across all worksheets*, including “People,” which is currently simplified.
----
h2. *4. Personal Data Risk Assessment Form (Template 4)* {color:#bf2600}*- FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt’s Preliminary Risk Assessment and DPIA template differ significantly from MODA’s prescribed structure. MODA’s template provides a more formalized methodology for scoring, threat evaluation, and classification.
*Recommendations:*
* Bolt _may_ continue using its global approach if risk criteria align with internationally accepted standards.
* If Bolt wishes to demonstrate close alignment, incorporate:
** Categorization of data importance levels,
** Threat/vulnerability evaluations,
** High-risk determination per MODA’s definitions.
----
h2. *5. High-Risk Response Plan (Template 5)* {color:#bf2600}*- FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
DPIA content directionally aligns with MODA’s expectations but *missing structured fields* required for a proper ongoing tracking plan.
*Recommendations:*
Add to DPIA (or create a dedicated local tracking table):
* Explicit *control gaps* field.
* *Responsible owner per mitigation measure* (not only project owner).
* *Deadline* for each mitigation action.
* *Status tracking* (e.g., Not Started / In Progress / Completed).
* Ensure DPIA includes *proposed mitigation measures* and *residual risk*.
----
h2. *6. Personal Data Incident Reporting & Handling Form (Template 6)*{color:#bf2600}*- FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt’s current two-document structure (Risk Assessment + Breach Report) covers most MODA fields, but gaps remain.
*Recommendations:*
* Use MODA’s *regulator reporting form* when notifying MODA—this is mandatory.
* Add:
** Explicit designation of responsible *personal data protection personnel* (“專人”).
** Clear *72-hour compliance tracking* field.
* Keep internal forms but ensure cross-document completeness aligns with MODA’s expectations.
----
h2. *7. Incident Response Notification List (Template 7) -* {color:#bf2600}*FOR ODPO*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt has partial equivalents (Excel regulator tracker + Braze logs + Breach Report), but these are _not_ a consolidated MODA-style roster.
*Recommendations:*
* Maintain a dedicated *Notification List (“清冊”)* including required fields:
ID / Entity / Contact Person / Phone / Fax / Email / Address.
* Add *MODA* as the designated authority for Taiwan (currently missing).
* Ensure this list is maintained as a standing compliance document.
----
h2. *8. Outsourcing Contract Template (Template 8) -* {color:#006644}*FOR PRIVACY LEGAL*{color}
*Baker’s Opinion:*
Bolt’s *DPA* already aligns with Article 8 of Taiwan PDPA Enforcement Rules and is appropriate as an outsourcing contract.
The *DSA* is controller-to-controller and not required for MODA purposes.
*Recommendations:*
Consider filling MODA-specific expectation gaps:
* Introduce a *pre-award contractor assessment form* (self-declaration of PD safeguards).
* Implement *periodic compliance confirmations* tied to contract term.
* Add clarity on *supervised destruction* and *data inventory* at termination.
* Review *liability structure*:
** MODA expects joint liability for sub-processor breaches (stricter than Bolt templates).
** MODA templates include punitive liquidated damages—Bolt does not.
** Decide whether to localize further or maintain current global stance.

----

h3. *Overall Baker’s Position*

* MODA templates are *not legally mandatory*, but MODA generally expects regulated entities to follow the format during audits.
* *Bolt’s global PD framework is strong and broadly compliant*, but several documents diverge in format, completeness, and locally expected fields.
* Baker recommends *selective localization*—focusing on areas most visible in a future MODA audit - outlined in the content above.

h3. *Next steps:*

# Flag feedback to ODPO & set up a meeting to align on next steps and prioritisation;

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account?

Hi Azza,

Thanks for the update and for adjusting the form.

To be fully transparent, I’m still not entirely convinced this is something the team should do from a relationship / expectations point of view. My main concern is that:

* asking drivers for feedback on Driver Score can easily be perceived as “you tell us what you want and we’ll change it”;
* whereas in reality some aspects of Driver Score are business-critical and won’t change even if most respondents dislike them;
* if we collect a lot of negative feedback and then visibly do very little, that can damage trust and feed the narrative that we “pretend to listen but ignore drivers”;
* This might create dificultes if, at some point, it is decided to have driver score with blocking in MT.

That said, from a legal perspective there isn’t a reason to forbid the survey, as long as it is clearly framed as an optional comprehension and feedback exercise, not a vote or a binding consultation. On that basis, we are okay with you proceeding, with a few guardrails:

*Purpose & expectations:*

The intro should be very clear that this is only about understanding and feedback, not decision-making, and avoid absolute statements and language that suggests this can never change. 

Your intro is already a good base, it doesn’t over-promise, and “where feasible” already helps. 

But I’d slightly tweak it a bit to:

_Dear Driver,_

_We would like to make sure that Driver Score is clear and feels fair for everyone. This short survey is to understand how you see Driver Score and to collect feedback that may be taken into account, if feasible._

_Completing this survey is entirely optional and will not affect your Driver Score, your access to the Bolt platform or your participation in any campaigns. Responses will be reviewed in aggregate to help us improve how we explain and develop Driver Score over time._

_Please take 2 minutes to fill out this form._

_Thank you!_

*Follow-up wording:*

Not sure if you have a follow-up wording, that appears when Drivers submit the form, but if you do, please avoid promising or committing to anything. Keep it simples, like _“Thank you for submitting your feedback.”_

With these adjustments, I don’t see any specific Malta-related legal risk that would prevent you from running the survey . My reservations are more about expectations management and future flexibility than strict legal constraints.

I also think we should ask privacy if they see any issue with this. [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] can you share your view?

Hey,

In Slovakia we have commission netting.

_Through commission netting, your campaigns/bonuses/compensations are reflected as a discount from your commission, instead of each having their individual invoices. Simply, your commission is reduced in the amount of your campaigns/bonuses/compensations - ensuring a more clear invoicing process, and less invoicing noise._

_For example, previously you would see a commission of 416.91€ and separate bonus lines of 11€ on your invoice, which totaled up to 361.92€. Now, you would only see a single row of commission in the amount of 361.92€, meaning the calculation is already done in the background._



Example for some [Driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/3318350?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]:

Taking November 2025 example from [Balance history|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/balanceHistory?balanceHistoryFilterSearch=%7B%22external_id%22%3A3318350%2C%22type%22%3A%22Driver%22%2C%22month%22%3A%7B%22month%22%3A11%2C%22year%22%3A2025%7D%2C%22viewType%22%3A%22monthly%22%2C%22week%22%3A%7B%22start%22%3A1762725600000%2C%22end%22%3A1763330399999%7D%7D]. 

Commission that driver had to pay is

{quote}*Commission = expense_cash_commission* + *expense_commission* (48.50 EUR + 190.83 EUR) = €239.33 EUR{quote}

this commission is ±20% of the amount driver had in Ride fees

{quote}Fees = *earning_in_app_ride_fee* + *earning_cash_ride_fee* (947.70 EUR + 242.50 EUR) = €1,190.20 EUR

Commission % = commission / fees = €239.33 EUR / 1,190.20 EUR = 0.20 = 20%{quote}

the [invoice|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices/5649895597?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] was issued for 132.94 euro, which is less than 239.33 because we do *commission netting* in Estonia.

{quote}*What is Commission Netting?*

*Commission netting* is a process used to simplify how drivers are invoiced for commissions, especially when there are bonuses, campaigns, or compensations involved.

*Without Netting:*

Normally, a driver would receive separate invoices:

One for the commission they owe (e.g., 20% of ride fees)

Separate invoices for any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations they receive

*With Netting (as done in Estonia):*

Instead of issuing multiple invoices, the system *reduces the commission amount* by the total value of any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations the driver earned.

The driver receives a *single, lower commission invoice* that already accounts for these discounts.{quote}

You can see discounts earned via cash and app rides in *earning_cash_discount_netted* and *earning_in_app_discount_netted.*

So we can calculate the final netted commission like this:

{quote}Netted Commission = Commission - *earning_cash_discount_netted - earning_in_app_discount_netted* = €239.33 - 26.70 EUR - 79.70 EUR = €132.93{quote}

132.93 is the same amount you can see on Monthly invoice (take invoice from November from [+here+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients/128179276?tab=partner_invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])

✨ That’s how you can calculate Commission Netting in Balance history.

Nikolay Roll

If you reissue an invoice and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices might get stuck.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Artem Lishchuk

The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) will take effect on 12 August 2026. Companies need to be prepared to meet far-reaching changes to the rules on packaging, packaging materials and packaging waste:

* *Stricter, uniform packaging design requirements:* Restrictions on harmful substances (e.g. lead, cadmium, PFAS), mandatory recyclability for all packaging, and rules on the use of recycled content in plastic packaging.

* *Establishment of a minimisation obligation:* Packaging design must be optimised in terms of material and volume, excessive packaging will be prohibited, certain single-use packaging (e.g. for seasonings and coffee creamer) will be prohibited from 2030.

* *Labelling obligations:* Standardised labelling of material composition (pictograms, QR codes) and information on producer, recycled content and reusability will become mandatory.

* *Extended producer responsibility and registration obligation:* Producers must register in a central register of producers and meet comprehensive reporting obligations; the definition of “producer” has been significantly broadened.

* *New obligations for online platforms and fulfilment service providers:* Online platforms and fulfilment service providers must ensure that all packaging placed on the market is compliant and must obtain all relevant information on producers.

* *Mandatory reduction targets for packaging waste:* Member States must gradually reduce packaging waste generated per capita by at least 15% by 2040 compared to 2018.

The German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety has also published a draft bill for a *new Packaging Law Implementation Act* (_Verpackungs-Durchführungsgesetz_, “*VerpackDG*”) to replace Germany’s current Packaging Act (Verpackungsgesetz) and to implement the PPWR in German law. Germany’s existing structures for the disposal and recycling of packaging are to be retained and built upon.

For a comprehensive overview of the changes that will be ushered in by the Packaging Regulation, read the full article on our website.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Also, the customer has already requested a chargeback on this transaction.

Thank you,

Hey [~accountid:712020:cb7d1436-9800-43db-821c-db7028a6ff03] ,

Thanks for flagging this and for the context.

*Regarding the campaign bonus:*

Given how close the two locations are and the fact that our system has flagged the second “trip” as fraud, it’s correct not to count this 170 m segment as a separate completed ride for the purposes of the campaign. Under the Malta Service Provider Platform Terms, promotions are only payable when the requirements are actually met, and Bolt may deny a promotion benefit where behaviour indicates participation in _Prohibited Manipulative Conduct_ (i.e. trying to exploit promotion criteria).

_“ 5.26.2. The promotion is subject to compliance with these Platform Terms. Bolt reserves the right to deny the benefit of any promotion where there has been a breach of these Platform Terms, including where a Driver’s behaviour indicates participation in Prohibited Manipulative Conduct.”_

So from a contractual point of view:

* the driver has not met the campaign criteria; and
* we are not obliged to pay the bonus or to make an exception here.


*Regarding the* *Driver’s behaviour towards Support / possibility to block:*

The Service Provider T&Cs also give us a clear basis to act on abusive behaviour:

* Drivers must not engage in violent, aggressive or threatening behaviour towards others; and
* there is an explicit zero-tolerance policy towards aggressive, intimidating or manipulative behaviour towards Bolt employees, partners or agents.

_“ 10.8. Bolt has a zero-tolerance policy towards aggressive, intimidating or manipulative behaviour. You must not, and must not allow any Appointed Drivers to, threaten, intimidate, dishonestly manipulate or otherwise abuse any employees, partners or agents of Bolt.”_

Bolt can temporarily suspend or restrict access to the platform where there has been a breach of these obligations or where there is significant harm to the integrity/reputation of the platform.

So yes, in principle we can take action (including suspension or, in serious/repeated cases, termination) if a driver is abusive towards Support. However, this should be:

* proportionate; and
* based on clear, documented evidence (chat logs, ticket history).

*Suggested next steps*

* Please save/export the relevant messages from the driver and see the exact wording.
* If the tone is rude / disrespectful but not clearly threatening or hateful:
** send a formal written warning explaining:
*** why the bonus was not paid;
*** that abusive communication towards Support breaches the T&Cs; and
*** that further similar behaviour may lead to temporary suspension or deactivation of access to the platform.
* If there are serious insults, threats or harassment, then a temporary suspension is justified, and in case of repeated breaches, termination of access can also be considered under the enforcement/suspension provisions of the T&Cs.

In conclusion: you don’t need to make an exception on the bonus, and you _can_ escalate the driver’s behaviour – just make sure we base any suspension/block on the actual messages and keep the response proportionate.

Thank you!

Hi [~accountid:712020:5f1385d0-93aa-434d-be59-3c34775dd55c]  

If you reissue an invoice and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices might get stuck.

*What is the solution?*

+*BACKGROUND*+

* In Spain, where a vehicle accident occurs and the rider requests insurance information, our current position is to not share the contact information of the fleet owner unless the FO gives written authorisation.
** If the FO does not give authorisation, we tell the rider to contact the authorities, and we will help once they reach out.
* However, in September this resulted in a rider escalating their [concern|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/642616928] as a consumer complaint.
** i.e., Rider wants the insurance details of the driver’s vehicle. Bolt reached out to the FO asking for consent to share _fleet_ contact information, but the FO did not [reply|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/642759420]. Rider want’s the driver’s details and the relevant insurance details.
** Rider has mentioned she is discussing this matter with her lawyer and the local authorities.
* *Request*: Can we share any FO contact information with this rider without the FO’s written authorisation?

+*THOUGHTS*+

* Our recently aligned position on such cases is [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0623C123AP/p1759498176854709?thread_ts=1759481265.650589&cid=C0623C123AP]. Namely:
** *Plan A* (initial escalation): Do not share.
** *Plan B* (where threat of escalation to lawyers/police): Still do not share, but direct them to the authorities.
* IMO this is tricky to maintain in all cases. EDPB guidance permits companies to share such information based on legitimate interest - IMO, we can share it in cases where the claim / need seems credible (i.e., where the balancing test weighs in the requestor’s favour), provided that we are sharing only what is strictly necessary. This is particularly applicable to this case, given the risk of escalation.
** The sticking point here, however, is that we have explicitly asked the fleet owner for their consent to share the information. This creates the strong impression that we are relying on consent, rather than legitimate interest. As such, if we shared the information and the FO was upset by this, they could credibly claim that we ignored the consent requirements that we ourselves set.
* In terms of where this leaves us, we have two options:
** *Option A*: Maintain our current position and do not share the details unless either: (a) we get consent; or (b) the authorities / lawyers write to us.
*** :green_circle: This is consistent with our general approach, and ensures we are not backing ourselves into a tricky compliance corner.
*** 🔴 This may result in further escalation / pain for us, and we may open ourselves to the accusation that we are trying to thwart the rider’s right to bring claims.
** *Option B*: Explore the possibility of sharing limited information - In particular, if the fleet contact details are *_business_* details, then we could argue that this is not personal data.
*** :green_circle: This would mitigate the risk of escalation / claims that we are thwarting the right to bring claims.
*** 🔴 The FO may be frustrated that we share fleet information without obtaining their permission.
* Ultimately, I think the following approach would be best:
** Check to see if the contact info is business-specific (rather than individual).
*** If it is, then: (i) send a courtesy message to the FO saying that we will share it, and given them a chance to raise concerns before sharing; and (ii) if we do not receive an objection, then share it.
*** If it is not, then maintain our current approach, as we have too explicitly relied on consent with this FO to date. This happened back in September, and seems to have gone quiet since then.
** In tandem, we should explore whether there are any other options for helping the rider here. For example, do we know why the FO has not responded?

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.
