Hi [~accountid:712020:7eb363dc-ca9f-4746-abde-3581e042a507] , thanks for escalating. 

Before we can determine whether this is an unauthorized access case, we need to clarify the source of the unrecognized charge. Not all unrecognized receipts or payments indicate that someone accessed the rider’s Bolt account. In many cases, the reporting person may be a victim of *credit card fraud outside the Bolt platform*, where another individual creates their own Bolt account and links the victim’s card to it. It is also possible that someone mistakenly or intentionally linked the reporting person’s email address to their own Bolt account.

To classify the incident correctly, please investigate the following:

# *Does the reporting rider have (or previously had) a Bolt account?*
# *Was the disputed ride made from the reporting rider’s own account or a completely different account?*
# *Is the reporting rider’s email linked to the account that generated the receipt?*
# *Is the reporting rider’s card linked to the account from which the order was made?*

If it turns out that the reporting person *does* have a Bolt account and the order was created from their own account, please ensure Tier 1 / Tier 2 followed the steps for handling cases where[ a user reports that someone has accessed their account|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/70724?country=global&language=en]. In such situations, the case must be investigated as potential unauthorized access and reported as a personal data breach.

Once these checks are completed, we can confirm the correct classification and next steps.

Thanks!

The acceleration_current_ramp_time for DC is 500 ms.

With the 350 W motor, ramp time of 500 ms felt safe. Even on steep hills, the front wheel lifted only when I intentionally pulled back on the handlebars. I also tested the ramp time of 2000 ms on the 350 W motor and the acceleration felt fast enough for me. 

However, for the seated scooter with the 500 W motor, the 500 ms setting is unsafe, as the front wheel lifts easily, posing a safety risk.

I recommend increasing the acceleration_current_ramp_time to 2000 ms for the seated scooter. With this setting, the scooter felt safe and the acceleration felt good (both 500W and 350W motor), and the front wheel lifted only when I intentionally pulled back hard during acceleration or going up steep hills.

Hi team, thanks for escalating this. Based on the description, this situation is very likely caused by *phone number recycling*, but we need to confirm the access method before classifying the case.

Please investigate the following points:

h2. *1. Confirm whether the reporting user recently changed phone number*

The user mentioned they changed phone number for some time.
Please check whether their current phone number was previously linked to a different Bolt account.
If yes, this would explain:

* why old orders appear under their sessions,
* why the balance (including a top-up for a past unpaid ride) was charged to them.

h2. *2. Identify which account actually made the 2023 order*

Please confirm:

* the *account ID* that created the 2023 order,
* the *phone number* linked to that account at the time of the order,
* whether it matches the phone number the user is currently using.

If the order belongs to a different user’s historical account, this strongly supports phone number recycling.

h2. *3. Check the payment method connected to the 2023 order*

The user reports they do not use Apple Pay, yet multiple Apple Pay payments appear in the history.

Please verify:

* Whether the *Apple Pay token* belongs to a different device than the user’s current device
* Whether the *device ID* associated with those orders matches any of the reporting user’s devices.

If the Apple Pay device belongs to another person, this again points to a previous owner of the phone number accessing that account.

h2. *4. Review login sessions for the account the user is currently logged into*

In Admin Panel → Login Sessions, please check:

* When the first login from the user’s _current_ device occurred
* Whether there were earlier logins from a different device before they contacted us
* The authentication method:
** Phone number login
** Cross-app
** Apple Pay session reuse
** Any other method that may indicate another person accessed the account previously

If sessions show that the user logged into an *already existing account* tied to their phone number, this is consistent with number recycling.

h2. *5. Clarify whether the user ever had this account in the past*

If the user confirms they never owned the account from which the 2023 ride was made, and we see:

* Older sessions from a different device
* Apple Pay tokens unrelated to the user
* A historical account linked to the same phone number

→ This points to *phone number recycling*, not unauthorized access caused by the user.

h2. *6. Next steps depending on the findings*

* *If phone number recycling is confirmed*
** Inform the user clearly about what happened.
** Log out all devices from the account.
** Archive the account that originally belonged to the previous phone number owner.
** If the user paid someone else’s debt (top-up), flag this to Fraud for reimbursement review.
** Raise a personal data breach ticket, because the user accessed another person’s Bolt account.
* *If the access came from a different method (OTP sharing, reused Apple ID, etc.)*
** Notify the original account owner.
** Log out all devices.

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

After making a [PoC|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/158383], we decided to reject this direction.

Respecting the grouping required picking a deliberate place for controller instantiation, so that it’s instantiated _before_ endpoint registration and it’s hard to get it 100% right, as there maybe different patterns. At the same time, it’s quite convenient that the code is appended at the end, so it’s easy to find the change within a potentially sizeable bootstrap. The engineer can reshuffle it later to their liking.

{code:sql}WITH owner_changes AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        created_date,
        MAX(CASE WHEN data_type = 'EntityId' THEN new_value END) AS owner_id,
        MAX(CASE WHEN data_type = 'Text' THEN new_value END) AS owner_name
    FROM fivetran_salesforcefood_spark.account_history
    WHERE field = 'Owner' --and account_id = '0017Q000018iNjPQAU'
    GROUP BY account_id, created_date
),

timeline AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        owner_id,
        owner_name,
        created_date AS valid_from,
        LEAD(created_date) OVER (
            PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_date
        ) AS valid_to
    FROM owner_changes
)

SELECT *
FROM timeline
ORDER BY account_id, valid_from{code}

To clarify the proposed framework:
If we apply all three metrics — *Driver Rating*, *Driver Score*, and *Acceptance Rate* — then a driver would lose access to Comfort, Premium or XL/XXL categories *only if all three thresholds are not met simultaneously*. At this stage, we would like to request your *legal assessment* on whether incorporating Acceptance Rate into these thresholds is permissible. From an operational perspective, both approaches are acceptable for us — using only Driver Rating + Driver Score, or implementing all three metrics.

However, adding Acceptance Rate would likely result in stronger performance outcomes and better service consistency, while also introducing certain risks. We would therefore appreciate your legal opinion on whether the potential benefits outweigh these risks and whether such an approach is compliant.

{quote}Dear [name],

Thank you for your follow-up. We appreciate your attempt to narrow the scope of the request.

Bolt does not generate or maintain the type of anonymised, aggregated dataset you describe for individual drivers. Our systems store individual rating events linked to specific journeys, and your overall average rating is calculated from those events. We do not hold a separate, pre-aggregated representation of this information for individual drivers, and data protection law does not require controllers to create new datasets or derive statistical summaries that do not already exist.

In addition, even an aggregated tally would still be derived directly from individual rating events that remain inseparable from the context of specific trips. Producing such a breakdown would require Bolt to extract and manipulate trip-level data that is protected under Article 15(4) UK GDPR because of the risk of re-identification of passengers. For that reason, we cannot provide aggregated counts or categories generated from those events.

To confirm, Bolt cannot provide aggregated or categorised breakdowns of individual rating events, and our legal basis for limiting access remains Article 15(4) UK GDPR as well as the principle that controllers are not required to generate new representations of personal data for the purposes of an access request.

Your overall average rating continues to be the extent of the personal data that can be disclosed safely and in compliance with our obligations.

If you have any further privacy-related questions, please let us know.

Bolt{quote}

Hi [~accountid:712020:8844fac2-7794-4fce-8945-42c254c5f728]  

*I reissued the invoice several times → But invoice still comes out with incorrect data?*

If you reissue an invoice several times and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code at least once (ie you get an invoice with a QR) → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices get stuck with incorrect (old fiscalised) data.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Nikolay Roll

Hey Team, 

We received the LSA’s new version of the contract. You can check it here: [^Copy of 09122025 LSA Malta Bolt.docx.pdf] 
For comparison purposes, you can also check our version here: [^Copy of 20251126 LSA Malta Bolt.docx.pdf] 

I will only highlight the topics that I believe that are critical. Meaning, they did other changes, but I think we can agree with them, reason why I won’t dive in:



+*Clause 5 (Fees) -*+ most of our protections were removed. Specifically: 

*a) Share of voice / loop lenght*

* *Our version (5(e))*:
** If total reel length of a digital screen increases and our Share of Voice (SOV) decreases, the monthly fee must be adjusted down proportionally.
* *Their version (5(e))*:
** “(e) The total loop length of the Advertisements shall remain the same during the Term.”

*b) Location changes due to MIA / operational changes*

* *Our version (5(f))*: detailed process if MIA forces placement changes:
** they must notify us;
** offer substitute placements of equal/higher exposure;
** we can choose;
** if no suitable alternative, we get immediate pro-rata credit;
** changes to one placement don’t affect others.
* *In their version, they eliminated all our text and inserted in the second half of clause 5(e) the following*:

_“The Monthly Fee will not be adjusted should any location changes during the Term by decision of MIA as mentioned in this Agreement. In such cases, the Advertiser will be offered an alternative Advertising Space of equal exposure. If the Advertiser chooses an alternative Advertising Space of a higher value, the Monthly Fee will be increased to reflect this amendment in the Advertising Space. If no suitable alternative is available, the client may receive a pro-rata refund for the affected period, but this will not affect the validity or continuation of the remaining Advertising Spaces. (…).”_

So, they *removed your structured replacement + refund mechanism* and reverted to their softer standard.

*c) Cost of reprinting / reinstallation*

* *Our version (5(g))*:
** If changes are mandated by MIA / operations and we didn’t request them, Concessionaire pays all reprint/reinstall costs.
* *Their version*:
** Only says: “_Any costs related to reprinting or reinstallation due to MIA operational changes will be borne by the Concessionaire, unless the change is initiated by the Concessionaire directly.”_ – but this is tied into their more general clause and without our  5(f)/5(g) structure.



+*Clause 8 (Remedies) -*+ They undo our amendments.

*a) Replacement / hampered space*

* *Our version 8(a)*:
** If a space is hampered/unavailable, replacement must follow the process defined in (our version of) 5(f), as outlined above;
** Concessionaire bears reprint/reinstall costs;
** If digital loop increases and SOV drops, fee is reduced per 5(e);
** Advertiser can’t claim _beyond_ what 5(e)–(g) provide.
* *Their version 8(a)*:
** Simpler: they can replace to comparable space;
** If no alternative, we get credit;
** We cannot claim compensation or cancel orders;
** They can leave ads on display after term.

They removed the cross-link to your 5(f)/5(g) process and our SOV protection here.

*c) Breach / termination*

* *Your version 8(d)*:
** Mutual: _“upon any breach by either Party… the other Party may terminate after 10 days’ notice to cure”;_ mutual remedies etc.
* *Their version 8(c)*:
** One-sided: only breach by the Advertiser (and failure to cure in 10 days) gives Concessionaire the right to terminate and claim remaining fees, keep deposit, etc.
** Plus a separate immediate termination right for non-payment of security deposit / fee.

They deleted the mutual breach clause and reverted to their Advertiser-only default.



+*Clause 9 (License rights and operational flexibility):*+

* *Our version 9* clarifies that:
** 1-month “Bolt Food” campaign right is already included in the agreed fees;
** No extra charge for using the same spaces for Bolt Food for that one month;
** Any additional Bolt Food campaigns require a written addendum.
* *Their version 9:*
Shorter and less protective:
** Says we _may_ advertise Bolt Food for one month, subject to MIA approval;
** Mentions we bear costs for artwork & upload;
** Does not say that this one-month Bolt Food use is included in the existing fee;
** No express mechanism for additional campaigns.

They removed your “included in the price” clarification and your addendum requirement for extra months.



Having in consideration that Carmen wrote in their email that “_Kindly note that we have incorporated whatever we can accept,_ +_and no more changes can be done_+_.”,_ please let us know your views.

Thank you!

** (i) Be presented to the drivers in good time before they are auto-enrolled (i.e., not on the same day);
** (ii) Have the effect of ensuring that their personal data is not transferred or shared as part of the auto-enrolment process (unless sharing certain limited data about the driver is a necessary pre-step, in which case please let me know), particularly in the case of drivers who have not previously enrolled for a pension and therefore their data is not currently with Aviva.

This raises a risk of both transparency non-compliance and driver complaints if they are caught unawares by auto-enrolment. +*BACKGROUND*+

* Yesterday, we received an email from a LT lawyer (Jevgenij Bogdanov).
** Letter head seems reasonably legitimate, and from a quick Google this person is a criminal lawyer.
* The letter is a request for information - specifically the telephone number of a passenger.
** Vilnius police is conducting a pre-trial investigation into potential criminal offence (bribery) by Jevgenijus Jankovskis (driver). Lawyer is representing JJ.
*** On 1 August 2025 (21:30), JJ was due to pick up a rider. However, JJ had an incident with a woman who stepped into the road nearby, and so was unable to pick up the rider. According to JJ, the rider would have been able to see the incident and could have testified about it.
*** CS seems to have located the incident [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2110696752/9?orderTryId=2620921680]. Although the trip details match up I cannot, however, see any internal notes suggesting an incident.
**** There are two trips from around that time. Other one is [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/2110704629/9?orderTryId=2620935824].
** “_In accordance with Article 48 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 44 of the Law on the Bar of Lithuania, I request that the telephone number of this client, to whom Yevgeny Jankovsky was to provide transportation services_”.
*** Purpose of requesting this information is to contact the rider and ask whether they witnessed the incident and would be willing to testify.
* The lawyer has apparently attached the attorney’s order (although I do not know what a real one looks like).
* It appears that CS has already prepared a response: [LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WDvMPuF3g2wTv-U4xW5NLEpp6rKyTvja/edit]
** Letter goes on about complying with law enforcement requests and privacy notices… not sure why.
** Letter provides full name, contact details and email of rider… not sure why. Definitely too much.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* *Validity*: Unconfirmed ⚠️ 
** Regional Legal needs to confirm the attachment / whether it looks legitimate :loading: 
** We need to see proof of authority to act :loading: 
* *Legal basis*: No explicit legal _obligation_ to disclose ✖️ 
** Article 48: Rights of the defence counsel. Does not require Bolt to share information ✖️ 
** Article 44: Right to obtain information. Specifically, right to “_collect, on his or her own, the data necessary for the provision of legal services which may be obtained by the advocate without applying procedural coercive measures, i.e. to obtain from persons the necessary documents or copies thereof or any other information necessary for the provision of legal services. The advocate’s request for information must contain proof of the relevance of the requested documents or copies thereof to the provision of legal services_”. This does not appear to *_compel_* Bolt to disclose the data ✖️ 
* *Proportionality*: Needs narrowing ⚠️ 
** We should not be sharing all of the details that CS has proposed- the lawyer is not even asking for it ✖️ 
** The same effect could also be achieved by email, rather than phone - the former is less intrusive. We should not be providing any more than the email 💡 

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Ask Regional Legal:
** Does the attachment look official?
** Does Article 44 compel Bolt to disclose?
* Ask CS:
** Are we confident that the trip and passenger identified are correct?
** If so, could we reach out to the passenger asking if they are ok with their email address being shared?
* Consider asking the lawyer for proof of authority to act on behalf of their client.
* *STEPS*:
** 1. Get Regional Legal and CS to confirm factual / legal points.
** 2. If we are compelled to share, and everything is legit, we share the email address.
** 3. If we are not compelled to share, then as a first step, we ask the passenger if they are ok with sharing. Be careful not to frame to heavily as obtaining consent - more a courtesy email. If they say yes, we might as well share.
** 4. If passenger does not comply or refuses, then we refuse the request, and refer the lawyer to the authorities (noting that we will comply)
** 5. If matters continue to escalate, we can reconsider. However, we should otherwise maintain this position for as long as we can.

We have found a root cause of the bolt and damaged thread issue. We measured the hardness of the forged top cap and found that it is not T6. The measured hardness value is way lower than the T6 should be and that is causing a situation where the thread is soft and the bolt with the glue is damaging it. We measured the hardness on our other parts as well and got the hardness value 15.

On the forged part the hardness value is max 12. In some small locations we got also 14.

Right now the PUSH-PULL test is ongoing - hopefully the part will not get broken. Final test results we will get next week {{2025-12-19}}.



We have informed BaoSong about it and asked them to check the parts in their stock.



CoEur told us that their part will have hardness minimum 80 HB that is equal to T5.

* *Art. 6(1)(c)* does not apply: the Law on the Bar allows lawyers to _request_ information but does not impose a binding legal obligation on private companies to disclose personal data.

*Proportionality & Minimisation:*

* Yes/no confirmation is the least intrusive means.
* Phone numbers/emails unnecessary — higher risk of nuisance; not required for the stated purpose.
* Trip data and behaviour data exceed what is necessary and must be withheld.

*Transparency:*
Bolt privacy notice covers sharing when necessary for legal claims; the limited confirmation here falls within reasonable expectations and is not harmful to the data subject.

*Outcome:*
→ *Permitted disclosure of yes/no answers only*.
→ *No additional personal data* may be shared.
→ This is a *one-off, low-impact disclosure*

_It was considered whether the Financial Support could constitute a cost to obtain a contract, as per IFRS 15. ​​The standard requires that incremental costs of obtaining a contract with a customer are recognised as an asset if the entity expects to recover them. [IFRS 15.91, IFRS 15.92, IFRS 15.93]. An entity can expect to recover contract acquisition costs through direct recovery (i.e., reimbursement) or indirect recovery (i.e., through the margin inherent in the contract). Incremental costs are those that an entity would not have incurred if the contract had not been obtained. [IFRS 15.92]._

_The Financial Support is considered as a cost to obtain a contract in scope of IFRS 15 as (a) the cost is incremental - only occurred when the Partner agrees/signs the Agreement, and (b)_ {color:#ff5630}_XXXXX_{color} _(Chicken Snack) expects to recover the cost indirectly from the Partner over the contract term (over_ {color:#ff5630}_X_{color} _(1 in this scenario) years). The exclusivity aspect increases the predictability of the revenue streams from the Partner and supports the view that the payment is part of the cost to secure future economic benefit._

_Given the above, the Financial Support will be capitalised as a contract asset (Deferred Cost) and amortised over the term of the Contract, which runs for 1 years._

I wasn’t able to find any earlier service or framework agreement with this provider, so it looks like we’re currently operating based on invoices and general industry terms. How risky this is really depends on how much and how often we use them.
Could you let me know the *typical value and volume of our orders with this provider?*
This will help us decide whether we can continue as is or whether it would be better to set up a proper bilateral agreement.

# *ELEA terms -* [https://www.elea.ee/elea-uldtingimused/|https://www.elea.ee/elea-uldtingimused/|smart-link]  

The credit agreement is subject to ELEA (THE ESTONIAN LOGISTICS AND FORWARDING ASSOCIATION 2015) standard terms. These are commonly used in Estonia in the logistics industry, but they’re non-negotiable, can be updated online at any time, and generally give the provider fairly broad limitations of liability. This is fine for low-risk, low-value situations, but it doesn’t give us much protection if larger amounts are involved. Depending on the transaction volumes, it may be worth considering our own agreement to ensure more predictable terms.

# *Pre-approval of invoice amounts*

The current terms require us to pay invoices in full even if the amounts differ from expectations, and interest applies if payments are delayed.
To keep cost control on our side, I’d suggest adding a clause requiring pre-approval of all amounts before invoicing, as well as clarifying that, if there is ever a conflict between the contract and online ELEA terms, the contract takes precedence.

*Next steps:*
Could you please confirm:

* The typical value and frequency of transactions with this provider
* Your thoughts on whether we should request a framework agreement between the parties to regulate the service, quality, and expectations, and liability, or if you feel comfortable proceeding as is
* If you could share an editable version of the agreement so we can add the adjustments mentioned above in point 3.

Let me know if you have any questions or if anything needs clarification. Thank you!

chiming in here from a Privacy perspective:

*Can we request the employee’s location history (July–December)?* Yes — but only in a proportionate, step-by-step way.

# *Ask the employee first*

* GDPR requires minimisation. We must request the information directly before looking at IT logs.
* We could ask her to confirm:
** Whether she worked outside Estonia since July.
** Which countries.
** Approximate dates or number of days.

# Our legal basis
Two bases apply:
Legitimate interests:
Possible misconduct (not reporting remote work abroad).
Need to assess tax and legal risks for the company.
These are genuine, documented risks and justify collecting country-level location history.
Legal obligation:
If she has created tax or reporting obligations abroad, we must determine this.
Establishing whether such obligations exist is itself a compliance requirement.
# Using IT logs (only if necessary)
If she refuses, gives unclear responses, or there is reason to doubt accuracy, we may review high-level login data (e.g., country from which she logged in).
This must be limited to:
July–December, and
Only the minimum information needed (e.g., country, not exact address).
# Bottom line
Yes, we can request the location history.
We must ask her directly first.
If needed and justified, we can verify via IT logs.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

*Parliament Passes Legislation Implementing Pillar Two Rule Amendments for Closer Alignment with OECD GloBE Model Rules*Parliament passed the amendments of the Minimum Global Corporate Income Tax Act (the Act) on 5 December 2025. The most important adjustment concerns the alignment with the OECD GloBE Model Rules, according to which the qualified Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) should apply when calculating the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT). To be able to apply the safe harbour rule, taxpayers must calculate the excess profit (tax base) subject to QDMTT based on the accounting standards used for preparation of consolidated financial statements of the ultimate parent entity. If that is not possible, taxpayers should use the accounting standards that allow applying the safe harbour rules. Under the current provisions of the Act, the QDMTT tax base is determined based on the financial statements prepared applying the IFRS or the Croatian accounting standards. Aside from that, the rules prescribe that the information needed for the calculation of the top-up tax (the top-up tax information return) will need to be provided using the template which will be subsequently prescribed based on the recently amended Act on Administrative Cooperation in Tax Area (which has transposed [Amending Directive to the 2011 Directive on Administrative Cooperation (2025/872) (DAC9)|https://research.ibfd.org/#/doc?url=/linkresolver/static/tt_e2_41_eng_2011_tt__ad9]).

The last significant amendment brought by these legislative changes concerns the procedure of filing a top-up tax return in Croatia where there are several constituent entities in the country. Let’s analyse. 
*1. Scope of What Bolt Actually Guaranteed* 

Clause 2(1) is extremely narrow:

We guaranteed *only*:

# *“Car rental fee each Tenant is obliged to pay under the Rental Contract”*
# **Casco deductible amounts up to *EUR 500 per vehicle damage*

We explicitly *excluded*: “any types of loss, penalty or damage claims of ABC Rent against Tenants arising under or in relation to the Rental Contracts.”



 *ABC’s Claimed Amounts*

✅ *1) Monthly rental fees: €14,480.24*

*Are they allowed to request multiple months per car?*
Yes — _but only if_:

* the amounts are *pure rental fees*,
* due under the Rental Contract,
* unpaid for *>30 days* after the invoice date (trigger under clause 2(2)), and
* ABC submitted the monthly report + written demand + Tenant confirmation.

*What to request before paying:*

* Full month-by-month breakdown *per vehicle*, invoice dates, and confirmation each invoice is >30 days overdue.
* Proof ABC delivered the monthly reports within the *5-day deadline*.

If any of these conditions fail → Bolt is allowed *not* to pay.

*Bottom line:*
We *generally must pay* overdue rental fees if conditions are met. But we can challenge:

* incorrect grouping,
* missing documentation,
* any amounts that are _not_ clearly “rental fee” under the contract.



*❌ 2) Early termination fee: €18,100.30*

An early termination fee does not count as a “rental fee”. 
It is a *penalty/compensation for early contract termination*, not a contractual “rental fee” nor a deductible under casco. Under clause 2(1), penalties are *explicitly excluded*.

If the amount is triggered by *termination*, not *rental*, it sits squarely in the “loss/penalty/damage claim” bucket → *excluded.*



❓*3) Insurance cases (8 cases = €4,000)*

The guarantee covers casco *deductibles up to €500 per damage*, but _only_ if:

* deductible is actually due under the policy,
* the Tenant confirms non-fulfilment,
* the monthly report includes it.

We need:

* *specific report per damage*,
* confirmation deductible was applied,
* deductible amount per case (max 500).

*Bottom line:*

Potentially payable, but only after documentation review.

If ABC is claiming more than deductibles → reject.
If origin of damage is unclear → request evidence and insurer documents.



❌ *4) Over-mileage fines: €20,012.70*

Over-mileage charges = *damage/penalty claims*, not rental fees.
Not included in guarantee.
De facto excluded by clause 2(1).



❌ *5) Tires for 2 vehicles: €1,760*

Tire replacement is *maintenance / damage cost*, not a rental fee.
Falls under excluded penalties/damages.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Afiba

+*UPDATE (12.12)*+

* I previously flagged to the business that we cannot collect BSNs on the back of driver IDs. We should aim in early 2026 to change the process ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1760370959919529?thread_ts=1755098033.151739&cid=C05NYVA7T2A]).
* The business asked: (i) whether we can collect BSN for AML/KYC checks, in light of PSD3; and (ii) whether NL banks can collect and store BSNs.
** I previously flagged that, since PSD3 will not come into effect until H2 2027, this does not really change my analysis.
* Earlier this week, compliance team hinted that the back of driver IDs are still being collected ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1765366500908269?thread_ts=1765364265.807489&cid=C05NYVA7T2A]).
** “_it was agreed to stop collecting the back of the driving licenses, however, the whole discussion was put on pause due to PSD3… The back has not yet been deactivated_”
** “_In the future we will need to re-instate the collection of the back since collecting a doc in full is an expected AML practice. We've also now received external legal counsel in NL about the BSN nr in regards to AML and it looks like in the future, we can collect the document in full (BSN nr must be visible for AML), but we shouldn't extract it to admin - i.e. make it consumable_”
*** Based on external counsel advice here, once AML changes come into effect (_in the future_) we will be allowed to collect the full copy of the ID (including BSN) as a financial institution (which Bolt will become in 2026 - [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D08K82MG5QW/p1765366926992059]), as we need to be able to check the document’s authenticity. However, the lawyers expressed “_some uncertainty around whether a financial institution can also store the copy ID with the BSN number, because, as they advise, storing the BSN by an e-money institution would likely not serve any statutory obligation_”, even though deleting BSN is not market practice.
* I advised that stakeholders that we should still push ahead with my advice ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1765542505619099?thread_ts=1755098033.151739&cid=C05NYVA7T2A]). My thoughts on this are as follows:
** (i) We are currently non-compliant, and are proposing to continue to be non-compliant for at least another 1.5 years (presumably). This will be difficult to justify in the context of a regulatory investigation.
** (ii) Even when these changes come into effect, it sounds like there is some legal uncertainty around whether we can *_store_* BSNs on our systems (even if we can collect them), and or logic here is simply “our competitors aren't doing it, so why should we?” ([here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C05NYVA7T2A/p1765366731685649?thread_ts=1765364265.807489&cid=C05NYVA7T2A]). As such, we should check this point with external counsel (I would like to be put in touch with them) - will we *_actually_* be able to collect and store BSN in light of PSD changes?
*** In short - *PSD seems like a relevant point, but I need to know how soon it comes into effect, and whether it genuinely means we can store BSN*.
*** For good order, I have also asked Kostya about this [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/D07AFGZ3V6F/p1765544802686809]. PSD is commerce-related, as he is preparing compliance in this area.

*Core compliance questions for the supplier*
{panel}

Based on the privacy analysis and Romanian-law requirements, here is the list of compliance items we need the supplier (iDrive) to confirm *in writing*. These should be forwarded as a single questionnaire. [~accountid:712020:ec09f884-709e-4d12-8b74-3045f0b19650] can you send them please?

h3. Data processing and security

# *Processing role* - confirmation that the vendor acts strictly as a data processor, with no independent purposes and no reuse of footage.
# *Server location* - written confirmation that *all* processing and storage occur exclusively in the EU, with no sub-processors or fallback environments outside the EU.
# *Security measures* - details on encryption in transit/at rest, access controls, audit logs, incident response timelines, and whether Bolt can request log exports.
# *Access segregation* - confirmation that the vendor’s employees cannot access footage except for maintenance under Bolt’s documented instructions.

h3. Product configuration and data minimisation

# *Retention configuration* - confirmation that Bolt can technically enforce a strict *24-48 hour deletion*, with no backend backups beyond that window.
# *Audio* - confirmation that audio recording can be *fully disabled at system level* and cannot be triggered automatically.
# *AI driver monitoring* - confirmation that all AI analytics (smoking detection, phone use, etc.) can be *disabled by default*, and that no behavioural analytics run unless Bolt explicitly enables them.
# *Video scope* - confirmation that the camera angle can be restricted to the vehicle interior only and does not intentionally capture the public space.

h3. Operational safeguards and ownership

# *Live streaming* - technical details about how live streaming works, how access is authenticated, and whether Bolt can restrict access to a defined set of users.
# *Deletion guarantees* - confirmation that deletion is irreversible and that data cannot be recovered by the vendor after the retention window.

h3. Documentation and compliance

# *DPA readiness* - confirmation that they can sign our DPA, including SCCs if ever needed.
# *Sub-processor list* - full list of vendors involved in cloud hosting, maintenance, monitoring, or customer support.
# *Privacy and legal operations document* - confirmation they will provide a clear description of how they operate from a GDPR standpoint.

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

* Fire investigations don’t just examine the moment the fire starts. Investigators often need to:
** Identify *early warning signs* (e.g., electrical faults, hazards).
** Verify *patterns over time*, like repeated overheating, blocked emergency exits, or unsafe behavior.
** Determine if the cause was *accidental or intentional* (e.g., arson, negligence). These patterns can develop *over 10–14 days*, not just 7.
** Some fire-related issues are detected *days after* they start (e.g., slow smoldering or structural heat buildup).
Also, if an incident happens before a weekend or holiday period, *a 1-week retention window may expire before an investigation even begins*.

Hi [~accountid:62b1c880566f3e7b0a8f2eb7] 
This is the analysis done by Privacy:
Articles 12 and 13 indeed do not constitute a valid legal basis.

 *Article 12*

Article 12 regulates _powers of NACP_ for lifestyle monitoring of declarants.
However, it applies *only to declarants and public authorities*, not private businesses such as Bolt.
It does *not* contain a rule obliging companies to provide information.

h3. *Article 13*

This defines the role of agencies engaged in anti-corruption activities.
It does not impose obligations on private controllers to disclose data.

h3. *Article 51*

Article 51 regulates _monitoring of lifestyle_ of declarants.
Again, the duties fall on the _declarant_ and _public bodies_, not on private service providers.

Nothing in these articles states that:

* private companies must provide _any_ data;
* companies must verify existence of accounts;
* companies must disclose commercial service data.

 

In short, there are no disclosure duties on the companies about Declarants.

Hi [~accountid:6233300873c8ec00699dc8b6] , I’ve taken a look at DE law and see that in Germany, continuous in-car CCTV recording of passengers is generally not permitted. These rules apply to the driver or fleet, because _they_ are the data controllers for any camera they install. Bolt does not install, provide, or operate CCTV equipment, and therefore is not responsible for compliance with CCTV laws.

*Driver obligations*

If a driver or fleet chooses to install a camera, they must independently ensure compliance with German privacy law (GDPR and BDSG). In practice, this means:

* continuous interior filming is normally unlawful in Germany,
* audio cannot be recorded,
* if any recording is used, it must be event-triggered and accompanied by clear passenger notice.

*Bolt’s role*

The new banner in the driver app does not permit, endorse, or encourage CCTV use. It simply collects a factual data point on whether a driver _already_ has a camera installed. Hi [~accountid:61374989bba6c7006a2616ba] ,

Thanks for raising this ticket and for information shared.

As discussed in our meeting, our considerations are the following:

* *Fake GPS fraud – Blocking/Suspension based on GPS use*

GPS-based indicators like speed or distance anomalies can be supportive signals, but if used as standalone triggers for blocks/suspensions, this may be viewed by courts as employer-like monitoring and disciplinary action, which strengthens reclassification claims.

In Portugal, GPS-related issues have been central in reclassification court cases. Courts have consistently held that the GPS is a key tool required to perform the service, which supports the position that couriers are dependent on the platform’s infrastructure to work — this has been favourable to us in rebutting the existence of an employment relationship.

However, if we start using GPS data as a basis to block or suspend couriers, this could be interpreted as Bolt exercising control and disciplinary powers, which could weaken our current legal position. The concern is not using GPS per se, but using it as the exclusive or automatic basis for blockings or suspensions.

Therefore, we think that any suspension/blocking related to GPS should be clearly tied to specific, proven misuse or fraud, and ideally corroborated by additional behavioural indicators — not GPS data alone. Otherwise, we risk reversing a court trend that has so far been in our favour.

* *Multiapping during active deliveries*

For multiapping, a system that merely flags behaviour and combines it with other violations could be justifiable, but never as a stand-alone reason for enforcement action.

Portuguese courts have also referred to multiapping as a positive argument for autonomy, consistently recognising that Bolt does not restrict couriers from working with other platforms.

Implementing a policy that blocks or penalises couriers simply for multiapping — even during active deliveries — could undermine this autonomy and create reclassification risk. We therefore cannot block couriers solely on the basis of multiapping. To proceed with blockings, we need to have some kind of T&Cs violation.

If there is still an intention to proceed with these initiatives despite the concerns outlined, we believe a more in-depth legal assessment will be needed.

Let us know if you need further clarification or if you have any specific questions that you would like us to answer.

Thank you!

[~accountid:712020:e27975af-e893-46c8-b231-c567323a57ac] - Thanks for tagging. [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425] has covered this well, but to add:

We should avoid defining what is or is not excessive since the threshold needs to flex with local dynamics and sensitivities.

The business can apply this commercially as needed, but should recognise that we reserve the right to limit access when drivers act contrary to the expectation that they use the platform in good faith, i.e. where they “significantly or persistently disrupt, interfere with, or delay the arrangement of Ride Hailing Services by other Users, or the matching of willing Customers and Service Providers by Bolt”.

If drivers are genuinely causing serious disruption to riders or to the functioning of the platform, there is scope to act. If the intent is simply to push drivers to operate in a way that suits Bolt, that may not be appropriate. A rule like allowing ‘only one cancellation in ten without penalty', would likely appear that Bolt imposes high performance requirements, I think.

A good basis for showing that a driver is acting in bad faith is clear and repeated communication that their behaviour appears excessive. Warning messages when scores fall demonstrate that concerns were raised multiple times before Bolt was forced to take action, which supports the fairness and proportionality of any measures imposed.

*Summary:*

* Local teams should avoid focussing on set definitions of excess and make use of the flexibility available.
* The clause should operate as a safeguard against genuine disruption, not a tool to compel preferred behaviour.
* We should not run into major problems if thresholds make sense in the context of protecting the platform and warnings have been used before suspensions.
* We will always face a degree of dispute risk on these topics, and the business will need to balance market performance expectations, with responsible management of reclassification risk and the risk of upsetting drivers.

Hey [~accountid:712020:9cfda827-f644-48a1-9da8-aff3fd427bf9] !

From a legal standpoint, we do not recommend sending SMS to couriers in Portugal for engagement purposes. This is mainly due to reclassification risk, which is still a sensitive issue in our market.

Direct SMS communication — especially if it includes behavioural nudges, incentives, or performance-related messaging — can be seen as a form of control or coordination, which courts may interpret as indicative of an employment relationship. 

For this reason, our external legal counsel has previously advised against using SMS, as previously shared.

Therefore, legal preferred approach would be using in-app banners and push notifications. These channels are less intrusive, easier to manage from a compliance perspective, and better aligned with our model of courier independence.

Please note DLA’s previous recommendations, where they express their view regarding direct communications with Couriers and specifically advise against SMS communication:

_“The existence of direct communication with the courier significantly increases the risks identified, because it shows that, despite the intermediation of the fleet, there is, in fact, a direct relationship between the courier and the fleet and decisions made by the platform regarding the courier's blocking, which shows, in addition to the direct relationship, the existence of control over the courier's activity and - more decisively - sanctioning power, which can be seen as the exercise of disciplinary power, which is a form of enforcing legal subordination._
_According to some of the court rulings we've already received in misclassification cases, which have dismissed the lawsuits and ruled that there is no employment contract between the company and the courier, the lack of a direct relationship between the courier and the company. (…)”_

_Regarding the communications to increase platform engagement, as previously mentioned, in principle, direct communication with couriers should be avoided, since the absence of direct communication between Bolt and the couriers – apart from the regular operation of the app – has been considered a sign that there is no relationship between Bolt and the couriers and therefore served as grounds for ruling that there is no employment relationship._
_However, and considering the impact that the lack of available couriers has on the operation, we believe that the risk may be decreased provided that:_ 

_The notifications do not show that Bolt controls the time the courier spends online. As a consequence, references as “We miss you!” and “Start today!” should be removed._
_The notifications are push notifications or in-app notifications, and not sent through SMS. Sending SMS to couriers is easier to prove and is a more direct form of contact, whereas notifications from the APP are exclusively linked to installing and/or using it.”_

We understand that the Team is now directly communicating with couriers regarding some campaigns and we understand the reasons why this is being done, but having in consideration that this risk is already being taken, we believe it would be better if we try to mitigate them as much as possible by not sending SMS.

Thank you!

Hi [~accountid:620b5eac156f53006b24766f] !

As already shared in one of our meetings, it is true that Article 185 of the Portuguese Labour Code, as amended by Law 13/2023 of 3 April, determines that if a fixed-term contract or a temporary work contract ends after the calendar year following the year of admission, the worker is entitled to:

* Full 22 days of vacation leave for the year of termination, regardless of whether they worked the full year;
* Full vacation allowance, equivalent to a month’s salary;
* Proportional holiday pay and Christmas bonus, in accordance with time worked.

This rule applies in addition to the usual proportional entitlements.

This means that, for example, if a picker started in 2023 and their contract ends in mid-2025, they are entitled to:

* Full holiday entitlement for 2025 (22 days + 1/12th salary as holiday allowance),
* Proportional Christmas allowance for 2025,
* Any leftover entitlements from 2024, if unpaid.

This creates an extra compensation cost to the agency, which they are now passing on to you.

In summary:

* The change made in 2023 grants extra compensation to workers staying more than a civil year.
* This type of cost is linked to contract termination and might be considered as fitting within the bucket of “caducidade/cessation” items.
* Can the agency pass this cost to Bolt? There is _arguably_ a basis for them to do so, since the law has changed and the contract does not explicitly exclude this type of pass-through.

Since the contract is not explicit (neither on our favour nor on their favour) if we want to push back, we can try to dispute their rationale from a contractual/commercial perspective, namely by arguing that:

* Under the 2022 service agreement and the commercial proposal, Bolt’s understanding is that all labour credits and termination-related costs are to be borne by the agency; and
* “Caducidade de contrato, FCT e FGCT” and holiday entitlements are already included in the agreed fee, rather than being charged separately.

On that basis, we can go back to the agency and ask them to indicate the specific contractual clause that, in their view, allows them to charge this additional “contract cessation fee” on top of the agreed price. And then we can try to dispute it following their response.

Please let me know if you’d like to take these additional steps.

Thank you!

5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under **Invoice tasks** or **Partner Invoices**.

Hi [~accountid:712020:3056969a-a5f6-4437-acfc-2cdfeb88a11e]  

*I reissued the invoice several times → But invoice still comes out with incorrect data?*

If you reissue an invoice several times and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code at least once (ie you get an invoice with a QR) → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices get stuck with incorrect (old fiscalised) data.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Nikolay Roll

Hi Lucca

From a reclassification point of view, nothing has really changed since 2023. These messages are meant to influence performance and behaviour which means they can be seen as signals of control. So the UK would face the same level of reclassification sensitivity as before.

*Bolt Standard/Principal model:* Even though more than 10k UK drivers have now been reclassified as workers, we have not actually changed our model or shifted our overall risk appetite. Management has not formally said that we are comfortable taking on more risk. If the UK GM is open to that, I can put together a detailed assessment that explains the risk of turning these messages on and what the consequences could be.

*Bolt Flex/Agency model:* I would not recommend using these messages under the Flex model. The model is already sensitive and under scrutiny. Even a small increase in reclassification indicators could cause problems. If the team still wants to explore this, we would need the UK GM involved and Legal would need to carry out a detailed risk review.

Let me know how you would like me to proceed.

Hello,

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

The page parameter is being sent as null in the API request.
Root Cause: The table state is persisted in the URL query string. When the page loads with a shared/bookmarked URL, the offset value is restored as null from the URL, but the limit value is missing (becomes undefined).

In line 101 of CarApplications.tsx:
page: input.offset / input.limit + 1,

When input.offset = null and input.limit = undefined:
• null / undefined evaluates to NaN
• NaN + 1 evaluates to NaN
• JSON.stringify({ page: NaN }) serializes NaN as null

A quick solution is to reset the search parameters and repeat the query.

On our part, we need to understand how this could happen and add checks for offset and limit.
{quote}

These are the points summarised, but take a look at the ticket as well as he has specific questions:
*1.  Uber/Lyft Comparison*

He asks why Hopp reduces the final payout when the toll changes, while other platforms do _not_.
He argues this makes Hopp less predictable, reduces trust, and puts financial risk on the driver.

*2. Route Deviation Responsibility*

He challenges the idea that payout changes are due to “driver deviation.”
He says deviations often happen because:

* Hopp redirects to Google Maps,
* Passengers refuse tolls,
* Navigation is unclear or unsafe (e.g., Hwy 407).
He asks why drivers are financially penalized for issues caused by the app or real-world conditions.

*3. Toll Fees & Earnings Predictability*

Even though tolls are reimbursements, showing them as part of “predicted income” creates misleading expectations.
He says post-trip reductions harm income stability.

*4. Kilometre Visibility*

He notes km are _not_ consistently shown on his acceptance screen and claims other drivers report the same.
He asks if this is a UI consistency issue and whether screenshots would help.

*5. Interim Driver Protection*

Since routing issues are acknowledged, he asks whether Hopp will *protect driver earnings* until routing is fixed (i.e., no penalties for app-driven deviations).

Hi team, [~accountid:5f4ce505d0884f0049200148] , thanks for your patience! Adding my thoughts from privacy side.

We’ve handled very similar setups recently in other markets, where Bolt facilitated accounting or self-employment services for drivers. The structure you’re proposing is feasible, but the documentation and privacy model depend heavily on who provides the accounting service, how drivers join, and what data we transfer.

Based on what you described, the likely building blocks are:

# *Driver agreement -* A written contract where the driver signs up for the accounting service. This usually becomes our main legal basis for processing and transferring invoice/earnings data.
# *Privacy transparency -* we will need to be clear with drivers as to:

* what data Bolt extracts,
* which accounting company receives it,
*  what they do with it (including filings to authorities).

# *Agreement with the accounting partner -* Depending on the model, I will help determine what agreements and with whom do we need from privacy POV.
# *Outreach / conversion -* If you plan to invite drivers into the service via email, SMS, push, or calls: this is treated as a partner offer, and we normally require opt-in consent before outreach or data transfer. If drivers discover the service in-app and sign up themselves, consent may not be needed.

To give you a precise list of documents and action items, could you confirm the below?

*Some questions to help speed up my assessment*

# Will Bolt _offer_ the accounting service, or will the accounting firm do so directly (Bolt only transfers data)? Have we considered only promoting the accounting firm, without being involved in the data transfer itself?
# Which outreach channels do you plan to use to onboard drivers?
# What exact data fields will Bolt transfer (e.g., monthly earnings, invoice breakdown, tax ID)?
# Will the accounting partner interact with tax authorities in their own name or strictly as a mandate-holder for each driver?

Once I have this, I can map the correct privacy setup and draft the needed agreements. Happy to jump on a call to align before you start building.

* *the GPS location of the accident* - as we track scooter and rider location during the order we also can say that we track GPS location of the accident. +*UPDATE (15.12)*+

* General:
** WfW has launched in Nuremberg, as a pilot. Intention is to roll it out further across Germany.
*** To implement this, we are partnering with a local fleet. WfW will be launched as a new category (G-Cars for Women).
*** In Germany, passports have gender field on them (but not drivers licences / ID cards).
** Generally, this is ok from a privacy POV. The main concern is with verification (i.e., proportionality of verification, and what we do with gender-fluid data subjects).
* Rider Verification:
** Process:
*** We will be collecting a copy of the rider’s passport (the only doc to have a gender field on it), and then comparing the picture against a selfie. 
*** Bolt’s systems will then compare the two to identify a match (in cases of exact matches, this system is fully automated; otherwise, there are fallbacks of human review for inconclusive results).
*** We are looking at both a face match and the gender field - the latter is a more recent development (see [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/5737709569/Sex-field+Check+for+Woman-Only+Category+v2]).
**** Unverified riders = ID verification + selfie (face match) + sex field check.
***** Veritas will perform the following checks: (i) Is the document real? (ii) Is it a real face? (iii) Does the selfie match the passport photo? (iv) Does the ID document have a field containing sex? (v) Is the gender listed as female? If these are all passed, then the rider can use WfW.
**** Verified riders = If sex field is female, then no changes (i.e., rider can continue to use WfW without interruption). if sex field is blank, rider is prompted to verify their sex in order to continue. If sex is not listed as female, then rider cannot continue to use WfW.
*** It is currently unconfirmed for how long we will be retaining this data, as well as where.
** Thoughts:
*** ⚠️ Legal basis: From a quick skim, it looks like consent may be needed. There are specific laws on copying ID docs (e.g., [+ID Law+|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_pauswg/englisch_pauswg.html#p0185]), and biometric processing will be involved here. As such, we would need to ask for consent. If consent not given, then we would need to: (i) do manual checks instead of biometric (which are in place already); and (ii) potentially not allow the rider to use WfW at all if passports are the only way of verifying (which sounds like this is the case). Ultimately, this should probably be checked with local counsel.
*** ⚠️ Proportionality: Although this is a grey area, we can argue that checking the ID doc is proportionate, as otherwise there is not ‘official’ way to verify gender - we would effectively just be eyeballing it (other methods would not yield the same results). However, we may need to be careful with how we _retain_ this data (ideal approach would be to extract the gender field and delete the rest. If we keep it, it must be clearly marked as a copy) - this will depend on what local counsel says as well as what systems we currently have in place.
*** ⚠️ Transparency: We need to ensure we are being specific and clear on why we are asking the rider for their passport, and what we will do with it. This will depend on the user flow.
*** ⚠️ ADM: We can argue this does not meet the threshold, as riders can use other categories (and human review element). However, the system should be robustly designed to avoid errors.
*** ⚠️ Discrimination: Gender is fluid, so some people may not identify with the gender listed in their passport. There is no easy solution to this - although not strictly a privacy issue, if we take a purposive approach to the feature, then we cannot allow them to use the category. They can use other categories instead.
** Questions:
*** The doc does not make it clear what exactly the user flow looks like. I am interested in whether we collect consent for any biometric processing - Can this be confirmed?
*** Please confirm how long we are retaining these pictures for, and where are we keeping them on our systems (e.g., Admin? GDrive? Beehive?).
* Driver Verification:
** Process:
*** Verification is being taken care of “_by our agents_”.
*** Per [+LSS-58536+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-58536], it sounds like we may be asking for gender during registration flow. However, currently unclear whether this involves checking things against ID documents,
** Thoughts:
*** It remains unclear what the process looks like in practice. Although this is lower risk than rider verification, we still need to check it.
*** It could be that the fleet themselves are verifying the driver’s gender - in which case, fine - but this is worth confirming.
** Questions:
*** What does the actual process look like here?
*** How are we sure that the fleet drivers are indeed female? Is the fleet owner assuring us of this, or did we previously collect any ID docs from those employees and check them?
* NEXT STEPS:
** (1) Business to confirm outstanding questions on both rider and driver verification.
*** Rider user flow?
*** Rider ID retention practices?
*** Driver verification process?
** (2) Check with Gab which local counsel we use - they can comment on ID document issues ((i) Is consent needed to collect and store passports? (ii) Is passport collection/storage likely to be disproportionate? (iii) Are there any fields on the passport that could raise local law issues for us?)
** (3) Depending on local counsel advice, we can adapt flows accordingly.

Hey,

In France we have commission netting.

_Through commission netting, your campaigns/bonuses/compensations are reflected as a discount from your commission, instead of each having their individual invoices. Simply, your commission is reduced in the amount of your campaigns/bonuses/compensations - ensuring a more clear invoicing process, and less invoicing noise._

_For example, previously you would see a commission of 416.91€ and separate bonus lines of 11€ on your invoice, which totaled up to 361.92€. Now, you would only see a single row of commission in the amount of 361.92€, meaning the calculation is already done in the background._



Example for some [Driver|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/3318350?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]:

Taking November 2025 example from [Balance history|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/balanceHistory?balanceHistoryFilterSearch=%7B%22external_id%22%3A3318350%2C%22type%22%3A%22Driver%22%2C%22month%22%3A%7B%22month%22%3A11%2C%22year%22%3A2025%7D%2C%22viewType%22%3A%22monthly%22%2C%22week%22%3A%7B%22start%22%3A1762725600000%2C%22end%22%3A1763330399999%7D%7D]. 

Commission that driver had to pay is

{quote}*Commission = expense_cash_commission* + *expense_commission* (48.50 EUR + 190.83 EUR) = €239.33 EUR{quote}

this commission is ±20% of the amount driver had in Ride fees

{quote}Fees = *earning_in_app_ride_fee* + *earning_cash_ride_fee* (947.70 EUR + 242.50 EUR) = €1,190.20 EUR

Commission % = commission / fees = €239.33 EUR / 1,190.20 EUR = 0.20 = 20%{quote}

the [invoice|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices/5649895597?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] was issued for 132.94 euro, which is less than 239.33 because we do *commission netting* in Estonia.

{quote}*What is Commission Netting?*

*Commission netting* is a process used to simplify how drivers are invoiced for commissions, especially when there are bonuses, campaigns, or compensations involved.

*Without Netting:*

Normally, a driver would receive separate invoices:

One for the commission they owe (e.g., 20% of ride fees)

Separate invoices for any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations they receive

*With Netting (as done in Estonia):*

Instead of issuing multiple invoices, the system *reduces the commission amount* by the total value of any bonuses, campaigns, or compensations the driver earned.

The driver receives a *single, lower commission invoice* that already accounts for these discounts.{quote}

You can see discounts earned via cash and app rides in *earning_cash_discount_netted* and *earning_in_app_discount_netted.*

So we can calculate the final netted commission like this:

{quote}Netted Commission = Commission - *earning_cash_discount_netted - earning_in_app_discount_netted* = €239.33 - 26.70 EUR - 79.70 EUR = €132.93{quote}

132.93 is the same amount you can see on Monthly invoice (take invoice from November from [+here+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-rides/clients/128179276?tab=partner_invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn])

✨ That’s how you can calculate Commission Netting in Balance history.

Nikolay Roll

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

Hi Team,

I've reviewed the case and everything is correct on Bolt's end. The preauthorisation was successfully released, and there is no further action required from us.

Please follow the steps in this Knowledge Base article to advise the customer: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7109163016850?country=global&language=en]

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

** Business does not see BSN as a high-risk issue right now. Given that it is tightly linked to the upcoming EMI licence and AML/KYC requirements, the business are hesitant to stop collecting the back of IDs, only to reinstate this practice early next year (this would result in a lot of operational friction).
** Gab recommended: (i) treating this as a medium-term issue rather than an urgent fix; and (ii) flagging our privacy position but leaving ourselves open to a phased approach rather than immediate removal of the backs of driving licences.
* During the call with Merili, Noud and Anneli, the following was discussed:
** Merili flagged that the EMI/AML changes will kick in at the beginning of 2027, as part of PSD3. Bolt’s compliance uplift in this regard will take place over the course of 2026.
** I explained our position from a privacy law POV - we are currently non-compliant by collecting BSN, and will continue to be so until at least the begging of 2027. As such, there is a compliance risk here in terms of data subject complaints / potential regulatory investigation.
** Merili flagged that although we will need to collect the backs of ID documents as part of PSD3 preparation (for AML/KYC checks), we only need to _extract_ certain information from this document. We currently extract BSNs in this context, but Merili admitted that this is for the purpose of duplication checks, and so is not something we necessarily need to do (driving licnece number on the front of the doc is already checked in NL and so is an option; alternatively, selfie checks could be explored). Merili acknowledged that we can stop extracting BSNs and listing them on driver profiles in Admin (although we would still retain the photographic copy of the ID, which contains the BSN).
** I flagged that there is obviously still a compliance risk here, given that we are collecting and retaining a copy of the BSN (albeit not on Admin). However, given that this is not currently a high-priority issue (as we have received limited complaints on this, we will need the back of IDs for AML compliance soon anyway, and the business are not interested in implementing changes unless urgent fixes are strictly needed), I explained that we can take a risk-based approach here and: (i) continue collecting the backs of IDs; but (ii) stop extracting the BSNs onto driver profiles as a duplication method. I explained that this not _eliminate_ the compliance risk but would slightly _mitigate_ it while we consider the compliance plan over the coming months.
** Merili explained that in Q1 2026, we will start to communicate compliance uplift plans to the business. Sam is already in the loop in these discussions, and I will be looped in when they become Rides-specific.

** Business will continue to collect the back of driver licences, but in the short term will stop extracting the BSN and putting it on driver profiles in Admin.
** When the PSD3 discussions become more advanced / linked to the Rides vertical, I will be kept in the loop so that I can continue to consider / advise accordingly.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

*I reissued the invoice several times → But invoice still comes out with incorrect data?*

If you reissue an invoice several times and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code at least once (ie you get an invoice with a QR) → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices get stuck with incorrect (old fiscalised) data.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Nikolay Roll

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 4 December, Portuguese rider ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/85329798/overview]) messaged Bolt CS ([here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/698026965]) complaining about “_charges for rides on my bank statement that are not in my ride history_”.
** Rider was in Japan at the time the rides were taken (9 Nov - 8 Dec), and so they claim to not have taken them at all.
** Rider flags that their card (used to take the trips) ends in 5286.
* Based on CS investigation, the rides at-issue were taken on this account ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/83558497]).
** This seems right - trips line up. All taken on card c6db7203-6dc1-4bd3-8264-b5639b423eb6 (last trip on 8 December).
*** Card is still active on the account at-issue. However, last 4 digits (8432) do not match those claimed by the rider. Card was added in April 2025, but not used until 28 October until 8 December. During first 50 attempts, driver did not respond for all of them - this looks suspicious.
*** There are a few active payment methods on the account, which could be suspicious.
** Account created a few years ago. Details have remained consistent.
* CS has already flagged to the complainant that the trips were taken on another account, and asked “_Do you know anyone named Diego, whose phone number ends in 6365?_”. The complainant confirmed that they do not.
* CS then wrote to the complaint that their account was compromised (it is not - this is incorrect) and that they would log the rider out of all devices (not sure why - this is not helping).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* It does *not* look like the complainant’s account has been compromised. Instead, it appears that another rider has somehow got access to the complainant’s card details, and added the card details to their own account for the purpose of taking trips. This in of itself is not a personal data breach, as there has been no breach of Bolt’s systems here ✅ 
* The only possible data breach here is in relation to the prices of the trips taken by the other rider. It is extremely debatable whether this is even a data breach, but it is worth reporting for completeness (I have done so [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0678KJ49UH/p1765816805586019]) - It is certainly not reportable ✅  

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Await ODPO confirmation that the breach is non-reportable.
* Ask CS to confirm explanation, and get them to tell the rider to block their card. This should resolve the matter insofar as it is no longer an ongoing issue.
* Escalate account to fraud team.

Once the above is actioned, then the ticket can be closed ✅
